talks.title: "Cursorless: A spoken language for editing code" by Pokey Rule (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how a spoken language built on Talon lets programmers edit code by voice using targets, modifiers and scopes.
talks.summary:
Pokey Rule, who has programmed by voice for several years after a repetitive strain injury made keyboards painful, introduces Cursorless, an open source spoken language built on the Talon voice tool for editing text and code. The argument is that voice differs from typing: spoken vocabulary can be composed into rich commands, but each command carries a small delay, so commands should chain together and reuse words people already know.

The core model has five abstractions: marks, which produce targets; modifiers, which pass targets down a pipeline defined by scopes; and actions, which operate on the final target. Targets carry attributes such as content range, removal edit and insertion mode, so actions like wrap, chuck, paste, bring, move and clone can behave correctly without special cases. Scopes come in dumb forms like token, line, paint and round that work in any text, and smart forms like argument, call and function that rely on Tree-sitter parse trees. The walkthrough builds up a single command that clones the first argument of every function call in a sample document.

Rule explains that this style is tacit, or point-free, similar to Bash pipelines and jq, and suits short interactive edits rather than large maintained programs. He closes with planned work: interactive tutorials, support in more editors, a richer grammar, bookmarking targets across commands, and using language models for actions or scopes such as sentences.

talks.title: "Using data-driven metrics to anticipate and prevent security incidents" by Caitlin Buckshaw
talks.teaser: Shows how GitHub's product security team turns incident data into trends, better preventions and variant analysis.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how GitHub's product security team set up a follow-up group to study bugs after incident response and the postmortem are complete. The speaker, who took on her first incident as incident commander after a bug bounty report that led to seven CVEs, notes that responders often move straight to the next case, leaving little time to ask how a flaw was missed and how to prevent it.

The team's goals were to capture data on every incident, spot trends across product areas, share findings with the right teams, and run variant analysis. Incident details flow through a Slack bot into GitHub issues, then into databases and dashboards built with Python and pandas. A scoring calculator loosely modeled on CVSS applies multipliers for repeated bugs in an area, severity, whether a notification went out, bypassed preventions, bug class and variants found. Findings are shared in biweekly discussion posts, biweekly meetings with engineering, bug bounty and security champion participants, and quarterly and annual reports. Reviews stay blameless throughout.

Variant analysis runs automatically when an area receives more than two bugs in a short period, and for high-risk bugs or those that bypass a prevention. A rotating working group combines dynamic and manual testing, code search, CodeQL, Brakeman and custom authorization tools, and documents results even when no variants are found. After one year the speaker reports more internal findings, improved preventions and stronger collaboration, while noting that the effort is effectively a one-person team drawing on many others and that limited time means not every incident gets this deep review.

talks.title: "Swift as C++ Successor in FoundationDB" by Konrad Malawski (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how Swift was added incrementally beside an existing C++ database codebase, bringing memory and concurrency safety.
talks.summary:
The talk is a case study of adopting Swift inside FoundationDB, an open-source distributed key-value store written predominantly in C++. The team wanted to eliminate memory and concurrency bugs that can become security issues, and their existing flow language, a C++ source generator limited to a single thread, was showing its age. Rather than patching C++, the goal was to replace it, so Swift was introduced incrementally next to the existing code.

The build was extended with CMake so Swift files sit beside C++ files, with Clang modules supplying the C++ headers. Swift code calls C++ types directly, and because both compilers emit LLVM IR, inlined C++ bodies can be optimized together with Swift code. Calls in the other direction go through a generated Swift header. A bridging header with annotation macros tells Swift how to manage reference-counted C++ types. Futures receive a protocol extension so they can be awaited idiomatically, and actors enforce isolation so that shared mutable state is flagged at compile time. Exposing actors back to C++ requires bridging boilerplate, which a macro can generate.

For debugging, the talk showed backtraces that span Swift and C++ and follow async suspension points, instead of stopping at the crash site as chained futures do. The speaker reported no performance regressions on the migrated core actors when measured with existing benchmarks. The takeaway for practitioners is that Swift can be adopted side by side in a large C++ codebase, and that compile-time concurrency checks and clearer diagnostics can justify the migration.

talks.title: "An approach to computing and sustainability inspired from permaculture" by Devine Lu Linvega
talks.teaser: Shows how running on a boat with limited power shaped a sustainable, self-hosted virtual machine for software that lasts.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that computing practice should be sustainable over long periods and matched to the complexity a problem actually needs, borrowing permaculture's focus on working within limits. The speaker has lived aboard a 33-foot sailboat for about nine years, with a few batteries and roughly 200 watts of solar power. Modern software drained those batteries quickly, while older environments such as emulated HyperCard, Think Pascal and a Smalltalk image ran faster and used less power, which prompted a look back through the history of computing.

Software preservation is another thread. The speaker cites an estimate that most commercial games written before 2010 are no longer available, and notes that platforms which host content themselves let work disappear. Strategies such as migration, emulation, encapsulation and targeting a stable virtual machine are compared. The virtual machine approach is tied to projects that stayed playable because their specifications were published and others could write their own clients.

This led to a small portability layer: a 32-opcode stack virtual machine with a Forth-style language, an assembler written in itself, and a toolchain that runs on the same machine. It was used for a game and for the speaker's website. Examples included assembly optimizations, stack-depth checking to catch errors, and controlled self-modification. The closing takeaway is to favor open specifications and understandable systems over adopted solutions, and to measure a project's complexity against real needs. The speaker is candid that the implementation is imperfect and that the ideas are the main point.

talks.title: "From Geometry to Algebra and Back Again: 4000 Years of Papers" by Jack Rusher
talks.teaser: Traces mathematical notation from Mesopotamian clay tokens to geometric algebra as a unified language for space and physics.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Papers We Love, Jack Rusher argues that modern technical mathematics suffers from fragmented, suboptimal notations and suggests refactoring mathematics around geometric algebra (Clifford algebra). Framing mathematical thought through an evolutionary and cognitive lens, Rusher highlights how human spatial planning—shared across hundreds of millions of years of evolution—provides an intuitive foundation that symbolic algebra should directly support rather than obscure. Drawing parallels between mathematical notation and programming languages, he traces historical shifts in numerical systems and demonstrates how geometric algebra unifies disparate geometric concepts across arbitrary dimensions.

### Key Topics
- **Evolutionary Origins of Mathematics**: How spatial navigation, physical planning, animal counting, and social deliberation evolved into geometry, number sense, and symbolic logic.
- **Evolution of Number Protocols**: The historical emergence and frequent philosophical rejection of new numerical abstractions, including fractions in ancient Babylon, irrational numbers, negative numbers, and complex numbers.
- **Notational Shortcomings and Fragmentation**: How standard Vector Calculus notations (e.g., Gibbs and Heaviside) obscure geometric intuition compared to formulations like Grassman's and Clifford's geometric algebra.
- **Geometric Algebra and K-Vectors**: How the wedge product and geometric product generalize vectors into higher-dimensional oriented entities (bi-vectors, tri-vectors, or general k-vectors), clarifying concepts such as imaginary numbers and rotations.
- **Projective and Metric Extensions**: How parameterized metrics allow modeling diverse geometries, such as Minkowski spacetime, conformal geometric algebra, and projective geometric algebra for graphics and physics.

### Technical Details
Rusher examines arithmetic and algebraic systems as functional protocols with generic dispatch. In historical Babylon, scribes computed areas and approximations (such as calculating the square root of two to six decimal places) using place-value base-60 tables of reciprocals and squares. Modern representations evolved past natural numbers and negative numbers to complex numbers, initially cludged by Rafael Bombelli from Girolamo Cardano's algorithms before being understood geometrically as planar rotations.

In standard 3D vector algebra, rotations and cross products do not generalize naturally across dimensions. Geometric algebra resolves this by defining three forms of multiplication: the dot product, the wedge product (producing an oriented bi-vector), and the geometric product (the sum of the dot product and wedge product). Through this formulation, the imaginary unit $i$ is revealed as a unit bi-vector representing an oriented plane of rotation. Extending the algebra with metrics allows unified modeling across dimensions without altering mathematical equations. In a live coding demonstration using Clojure and Emacs, Rusher shows how a physics simulation accounting for gravity, Hooke's law, and damping operates identically across 2D, 3D, and 4D spaces simply by changing the dimensionality parameter.

### Takeaways
Rusher advocates for adopting geometric algebra across physics, engineering, and computer graphics, pointing to David Hestenes' research program and 2002 Oersted Medal lecture. Unifying technical mathematics under geometric algebra eliminates redundant tools (such as isolated cross products, Pauli/Dirac matrices, and quarternions), which could reduce physics education by several years while making advanced spatial and physical concepts vastly more accessible and intuitive.

talks.title: "Concatenative programming and stack-based languages" by Douglas Creager
talks.teaser: Compares stack-based languages with name-based ones, then shows how they reach Turing completeness and compile to assembly.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces stack-based languages as a family of programming languages that most developers have not encountered, defined by the absence of named values. The speaker starts with a Python program that computes a triangle's hypotenuse using variables and a function, and walks through how environments and call frames grow and get discarded during evaluation. The same logic is then rewritten for a stack machine, where literals push onto a stack and operators pop their operands. Extra instructions such as dup, swap and dig are needed to reorder values, and quotations with an apply instruction stand in for functions.

The middle section covers the formal meaning of these programs. Stack effect notation, which originated in Forth and was extended by Factor, describes how a program changes the stack. A more rigorous definition treats each program as a stack transformer, where sequential concatenation corresponds to function composition, and that property makes the composition associative. Turing completeness is argued by reducing the Lambda calculus through combinatory logic (S, K and I) to a stack language, and the instruction set is then reduced to a minimal basis. Associativity is shown to allow splitting a program into chunks, compiling each one to x86 assembly in parallel, and concatenating the results.

The talk closes with uxn, a real stack-based language with its own virtual machine, shown running a snake game, a clock and pong on an emulator and on a small device. The main takeaway is that stack languages are conceptually simple, which makes them well suited to implementation on constrained hardware.

talks.title: "Programming Distributed Systems" by Mae Milano
talks.teaser: Surveys research on programming languages that tackle data races, consistency and ownership in distributed systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the difficulty of programming distributed systems, where familiar abstractions keep leaking and new bugs and vulnerabilities keep appearing. The speaker frames three problems: destructive data races in shared memory, coordination overhead from strongly consistent replication, and consistency errors that arise when replicas diverge under weak guarantees. Each is illustrated with a simple example before any solution is offered.

To address consistency, the talk presents a transactional language that lets each transaction run at the weakest consistency it can tolerate. Its compiler applies an information flow type system to reject programs where strongly consistent results depend on weakly consistent data. An online game example, with win and loss tables and a tournament invitation, shows a ranking transaction that the compiler flags. The talk then covers monotonic data such as counters and sets that only grow, which let programs stay correct under weak consistency without coordination. A stable message delivery protocol is used to show how this works in a replicated setting.

For data races, the talk looks at type systems that enforce mutual exclusion at compile time. It contrasts Rust's restriction to tree-shaped references with a region-based approach that permits structures such as doubly linked lists, using an isolation keyword and dynamic checks where static analysis is not enough. The takeaway for practitioners is that better language design can rule out whole classes of concurrency bugs, though some shared state still needs transactions or locks.

talks.title: "Didn't Chrome Already Have a Root Store?" by David Adrian (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explains why Chrome built its own root store and certificate verifier, and how that shifts web PKI trust toward automation.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from why the web needs more than encryption: a browser also has to know that a certificate belongs to the site it names. It explains digital signatures, how certificates bind a name to a public key, and how browsers and platform vendors trust certificate authorities through root stores and root programs. Past incidents such as DigiNotar and the WoSign and StartCom backdating cases show why these trust decisions matter.

Chrome originally relied on platform verifiers and root stores, which behaved inconsistently in distrust and edge cases. Chrome's own root store and verifier, launched in Chrome 105, gave consistent results across platforms. The rollout surfaced platform quirks, including Windows drawing trust from many locations and macOS keychain calls that could hang the browser. Measurements showed fewer certificate errors, largely on older Windows machines that lacked updated roots, and slightly faster page loads.

The Chrome root program aims for security through agility and simplicity, mainly via automation. The speaker walks through the certificate authority lifecycle of domain validation, issuance and status. Automated ACME validation shortens how long a validation can be reused, and multi-perspective validation hardens it against DNS and BGP attacks. Because OCSP is costly and leaks browsing data, Chrome proposed making it optional, requiring CRLs, and allowing certificates of ten days or less that need no revocation tracking. The takeaway is that automation and shorter lifetimes are the levers for keeping the web PKI secure, including through future post-quantum migrations.

talks.title: "Building Strong and Sustainable Open Source Projects" by Lawrence Gray (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Uses road trip stories to explain how open source projects build governance, community, and sustainability.
talks.summary:
Lawrence Gray opens with a road trip he took with a friend after their summer internships, heading toward Vancouver on very little money. The trip was full of unplanned turns, including a family dinner, a house party, and days spent with strangers who offered food and beds. Gray uses these episodes to frame what a successful open source project needs: a clear purpose, openness to diversity, resilience after setbacks, and shared ownership of achievements.

The practical advice comes next. Projects should build a governance model, create spaces for discussion, and document things at three levels: user tutorials, contributor guides, and code documentation. To counter burnout, Gray's project runs three-month terms in which members sign up for a role and can step away without obligation. To stay engaged, projects can give conference talks, host local meetups and community hackathons, bring open source into university courses, offer mentorship, and take part in programs such as Google Summer of Code. Gray also recommends fiscal sponsorship through NumFOCUS for managing funds, and warns against ignoring user feedback, setting too many contributor rules, or neglecting the community.

A second story, a hitchhiking trip around Tasmania, illustrates how strangers can form a trusting network. The talk closes by encouraging listeners to submit a first pull request to a project they already use. The audience questions covered fundraising, settling bikeshedding disputes through trusted decision makers, handing off a project when burned out, corporate-led open source, and whether contributors can be paid.

talks.title: "The Economics of Programming Languages" by Evan Czaplicki (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores how corporate, independent, and open source programming languages get funded, and how that funding shapes their design.
talks.summary:
The designer of Elm opens by describing more than ten years of maintaining a language, where the work grew from compiler engineering into package infrastructure, releases across platforms, community events, trademarks and foundation governance. He asks who pays for this work and why, and starts with the money flowing into browsers. He explains how search engines pay to be the default search in browsers, and how that payment makes the search bar work like a landlord collecting rent from storefronts. He backs this with the scale of the payments and the browser market shares involved.

He then sorts language funding into corporate models, such as a company-controlled platform, a corporate alliance that negotiates standards, and rewarding talent, and independent models, such as patronage, consulting, research grants, editor or usage licenses, hosting, and donations. For each one he weighs design incentives, such as whether a feature should be added, and career risks, such as depending on a funder whose goals can change. He shares his own experience with patronage, where a funder's priorities shifted and his work was no longer valued. He also describes a hosting idea that compiles Elm to C and SQL for Postgres, which he has prototyped but worries that larger cloud providers could copy.

He closes by asking authors, users and the wider community to consider a language's goals, its author's situation and the trade-offs before adopting it. He leaves open whether the search-based rent model is harmful and how small authors could address switching costs.

talks.title: "Lessons from building GitHub code search" by Luke Francl (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explains how GitHub rebuilt its code search engine to index billions of files faster and support regex at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk traces why GitHub's original code search was slow, limited in what it could match, and unable to index forks. Indexing ran through a monolithic Ruby stack, and the tokenizer stripped out programming characters, so the team had to weigh trigram indexing against its storage and rebuild costs. The old system ran on 312 servers and took months to re-index, which discouraged experimentation.

The replacement, a Rust-based engine called Blackbird, used an event-driven crawler, a Kafka buffer, and a cache server that reused prior index work. To handle forks, the team deduplicated content by git blob ID and used a minimum spanning tree over repository similarity to order Delta compression. Estimating differences between repositories was a challenge because HyperLogLog accuracy depends on set size, so the team turned to a geometric xor filter, which estimates symmetric difference relative to the size of the change. Dynamic shard assignment moved compaction onto separate hosts, and each shard gained a second replica for redundancy.

The final system ran on about 130 servers across three redundant clusters, with the cache reaching a hit rate above 99.9 percent during full rebuilds. Because a rebuild takes days rather than months, the index format has changed 50 times in three years. The main takeaways: custom infrastructure can beat off-the-shelf tools when you exploit your data's structure, scaling problems recur at each order of magnitude, and designing for change pays off in delivered features.

talks.title: "Making Hard Things Easy" by Julia Evans (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores why basic computing topics like bash, HTTP, SQL and DNS feel so hard to learn, and how to make them easier.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Strange Loop 2023, Julia Evans discusses why computing concepts that seem basic—such as Bash, HTTP, SQL, and DNS—often take years to master. Drawing from her experience founding Wizard Zines to demystify complex computing systems, Evans emphasizes that technical friction is rarely a personal failing. Instead, it stems from systemic factors such as piles of obscure gotchas, massive underlying codebases, hidden internal mechanics, and unintuitive tooling outputs. She examines practical mental models, heuristics, and community roles that help make hard topics easier to learn and navigate.

### Key Topics
Evans breaks down why four foundational technologies are unexpectedly difficult and provides strategies to simplify them:
- **Bash and Hidden Gotchas**: Bash is an infrequently used language full of edge cases and trivia. A small script demonstrates how `set -e` fails to exit on errors when functions are used in compound statements like logical OR (`||`), which globally disables `set -e` inside the called function. Tools like ShellCheck offload trivia from human memory, while sharing real-world failure stories helps engineers decide when to avoid problematic patterns.
- **HTTP and Accidental Complexity**: HTTP structures appear straightforward (status code, headers, body), but understanding them requires dealing with browsers containing over 20 million lines of code and evolving security models. Rather than memorizing all 40+ HTTP request headers or entire command-line man pages (like `grep`), Evans advocates pruning large lists down to small, human-scale subsets of high-value items, paired with honest, reliable references such as MDN and official RFCs.
- **SQL and Chronological Execution**: In SQL, query syntax does not match execution order. Demystifying SQL requires asking what the computer executes first chronologically (e.g., `FROM` -> `WHERE` -> `GROUP BY` -> `HAVING` -> `SELECT` -> `ORDER BY` -> `LIMIT`). Evans notes that tracing chronological sequences also clarifies topics like CORS message exchanges, process startup (`behind hello world on Linux`), and cross-team service workflows.
- **DNS and Hidden Mechanics**: DNS is hard because intermediate library code, local and upstream caches, and communications between resolvers and authoritative name servers are invisible. To illuminate these hidden interactions, Evans and her friend Marie built "Mess with DNS," an authoritative name server that displays incoming resolver queries in real time. For confusing terminal tools like `dig +norecurse`, she recommends "eraser eyes"—filtering out visual noise to focus strictly on actionable signals (such as `SERVFAIL` indicating a cache miss).

### Technical Details
- **Shellcheck & Bash traps**: In Bash, constructs such as `my_function || echo 'failed'` disable `set -e` inside `my_function`, bypassing standard error termination behavior.
- **DNS Inspection**: Using `dig +norecurse` allows querying a recursive resolver specifically for cached data, where a `SERVFAIL` response indicates the resolver does not hold cached records for the query.
- **Interactive Visualizers**: Tools like `mess with DNS` and `float.exposed` expose hidden system mechanics (e.g., DNS resolver traffic patterns or spacing between IEEE 754 32-bit floating-point values) to build intuition.

### Takeaways
Difficulty in understanding foundational systems is normal and driven by hidden state, complex distributed architectures, and unintuitive outputs. Evans highlights the community ecosystem required to demystify technology: the "Grumpy Old Timer" sharing past failure modes, the "Loud Newbie" asking clarifying questions without fear of judgment, the "Bug Chronicler", the "Tool Builder", the "Today I Learned" sharer, people who answer questions, and the "Documentarian" who writes it all down. By identifying the exact reasons a system is hard, developers can create tools, prune information, and trace execution to make hard things easy.

talks.title: Brittany Johnson-Matthews: Causal testing: understanding the root causes of defects
talks.teaser: Shows how causal testing turns a failing test into minimally different passing and failing runs that expose a defect's cause.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a study of why developers adopt or avoid software tools. Its main complaints were hard-to-digest tool output, tool design problems, and workflow integration overhead. Follow-up work in testing noted that conventional tests can show that a defect exists and sometimes where it sits, but rarely why the behavior happened.

Causal testing is presented as a way to answer that why question using test cases a team already has. Starting from a failing test, the method perturbs its inputs to generate new valid tests, runs them, and sorts the results into passing and failing sets. Those are then compared with the original using both inputs and execution paths, so the most similar passing and failing tests point to the cause. In a directions example, the passing tests started and ended in the same country while the failing ones did not, which quickly suggested the cause. The talk also covers two extensions: causal fairness testing, which flips one attribute at a time, such as race in a loan decision tool, to measure how often outcomes change because of that attribute; and testing machine learning-based software with assertions that check whether outputs stay equal when an input such as a name changes.

A proof-of-concept implementation was evaluated with participants, who reported that the similar passing tests pointed to the cause and that the approach helped them find and fix root causes. The practical takeaway is that causal testing adds explanatory insight to existing code and tests without requiring much extra effort, and the speaker invites discussion on fitting it into a team's testing process.

talks.title: Shane McIntosh: The unintended consequences of mining software build systems
talks.teaser: Presents Build Medic, a tool that automatically repairs broken build scripts, and the noisy build data that complicates its evaluation.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar frustration: a Maven build fails after a dependency's coordinates change, such as Log4j being referenced differently in Maven Central, and the fix has to be made by hand. The speaker asks why build systems cannot sustain themselves. A self-sustaining build would need tools that detect underspecified dependencies, anticipate necessary build changes, and automatically apply fixes to build scripts. The talk focuses on the last of these, automated repair.

The speaker presents Build Medic, which takes a build failure log, classifies the kind of failure, selects a repair strategy, applies it, and re-evaluates the build. If the build still fails, it loops back to try another fix. On 84 unseen breakage pairs mined from open source commit history, a little more than half were fixed automatically, and about three quarters of those were fixed in a single iteration. In the correct fixes, about a third matched the developers' change exactly, and 44 percent modified the same elements in a slightly different way.

The speaker then questions the evaluation, which assumes historical breakages are important and that developers rush to fix them. About 12 percent of passing builds had at least one actively ignored failing job, sometimes up to 87 percent of failing jobs. Roughly two-thirds of failing builds were stale, with fix times ranging from a day to years. The speaker offers two conclusions: either the evaluation is right and build data is noisy, which calls for measuring and tracking that noise, or the evaluation is flawed, and developers are invited to help improve it.

talks.title: Kelly Blincoe: The effects of destructive criticism in code review
talks.teaser: Shows how destructive code review feedback lowers developers' motivation to keep working and their willingness to improve code.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a study of how developers perceive destructive criticism in software code review, meaning feedback that is inconsiderate and non-specific. The researchers used an online questionnaire built on vignettes. Participants imagined submitting a code snippet and receiving either constructive or destructive feedback on it, and they answered questions about each version.

Destructive feedback was seen as less appropriate and less likely to help improve the code, even when participants found it valid. After receiving it, participants reported much lower motivation to keep working on the task, with the developer, and on the project as a whole. Women reported being less motivated to keep working with the developer and on the project after destructive feedback. Less experienced developers were more likely to apologize and agree with harsh comments, while more experienced developers were more likely to say the feedback should be more considerate. Respondents reported receiving destructive criticism far more often than giving it: 22 percent said they had received some in the past year, while about one percent said they had given it. Opinions were split on whether inconsiderate feedback was acceptable if it improved the code.

The takeaway is that how people are treated affects whether code gets improved and whether developers stay on a project. Teams need ways for reviewers to learn when their feedback lands badly, should adapt feedback to what each recipient prefers, and should think carefully before criticizing someone in a public venue rather than privately.

talks.title: Christoph Treude: Automatically enhancing error messages
talks.teaser: Shows how crowdsourced Stack Overflow answers can be turned into clearer Python compiler error messages inside the IDE.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short Python script that tries to remove duplicates from a list using dict.fromkeys. It fails with a message claiming the list is not callable, which the speaker argues describes what the interpreter attempted rather than what the programmer was trying to achieve. He traces this complaint back to a 1976 paper on language design. A web search for a fix usually leads to a Stack Overflow thread, where the accepted answer explains that naming a variable list shadows a built-in name.

The middle of the talk presents Pycee, a prototype that enhances Python error messages. It parses the error, builds a Stack Overflow query depending on the error type, and selects an answer using signals such as acceptance, presence of code and votes. It then replaces variable names in that answer with the names the user actually used and summarizes long responses into a short hint, so the IDE can show a more actionable explanation.

To evaluate the approach, the researchers had 16 professional developers complete two practice exercises each, with one task using Pycee and the other using the official Python documentation as a baseline. Across 115 encountered errors, participants rated the enhanced messages as more helpful, while their agreement that the messages saved time was less pronounced. The takeaway is to crowdsource error explanations and use automated filtering to separate correct answers from incorrect ones.

talks.title: Maurício Aniche: How code coverage can be used and abused to guide testing.
talks.teaser: Argues that code coverage helps developers decide where to add tests, and reviews research on its limits as a quality target.
talks.summary:
The talk defends code coverage against common complaints, such as that it can be gamed, pushes developers into pointless tests, or hides weak assertions. The speaker argues the metric is useful when it is used properly. A developer writes tests from the specification while building a feature, then runs a coverage tool and asks why each uncovered line was missed. Coverage informs whether more tests are worth writing, but it should not make that call, and tests should never be added just to lift the number.

Next the speaker reviews research on coverage and test effectiveness. A 1994 study by Hutchins and colleagues found that suites above about 90 percent coverage detected faults better than weaker ones, while full coverage alone did not guarantee good tests. A 2009 study found that targeting code not yet exercised found new faults more effectively than adding tests for already covered code. Another paper concluded that coverage reliably flags under-tested areas but performs poorly as a quality target.

For criteria, the speaker suggests statement coverage is enough for most teams, since any tool can measure it in any language, instead of chasing complex criteria like MC/DC or path coverage. The takeaways: use coverage to augment a suite, never set it as a fixed target, and remember that high coverage does not prove quality while low coverage is a clear warning sign.

talks.title: Marieli Wessel: How people really use GitHub Actions
talks.teaser: Presents a study of GitHub Actions usage across thousands of projects and what adopting them changes in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by explaining GitHub Actions as a way to automate repository work, with workflows triggered by events such as new branches, comments and pull requests, and with actions that can be shared between repositories. Actions are written as configuration files that should be handled like code, but the speaker argues that teams often do not treat them that way.

The study examined the configuration files of about 3,000 projects and found roughly 700 distinct actions in 20 categories. The most common were continuous integration, utilities, deployment, publishing and code quality. A typical action was added and then never removed or modified, while a few specific actions had their arguments changed many times. Discussions among developers focused on how actions are maintained, how to build custom ones, and moving from other CI/CD tools to actions. The speaker also compared repositories before and after adoption and found two consistent effects: more pull requests were rejected, and merged pull requests were required to have fewer commits.

The main takeaway is that adopting an action means taking on a new dependency that needs ongoing upkeep, and that it can change how contributors work together. The speaker recommends measuring code performance and community metrics before and after introducing actions, so teams can spot unexpected effects early.

talks.title: Matthias Galster: Value and waste in software engineering
talks.teaser: Surveys research on software waste, code review smells, technical debt fixing, and turning human values into product requirements.
talks.summary:
The talk draws on a special issue on value and waste in software engineering and argues that these ideas are hard to act on without concrete definitions. It opens with a study that defined waste in software engineering and sorted it into nine categories, each with its causes, which teams can use when discussing and planning their work.

The speaker then gives three examples. First, poor code reviews create waste. The research names review smells such as approvals that skip real review, reviews handed to friends rather than used for knowledge sharing, back-and-forth ping-pong exchanges, unanswered reviews, oversized change sets and missing context. These lead to rework, waiting and high cognitive load. Second, technical debt is not fixed the same way across types. Code and defect debt are usually fixed by the developer who introduced them, while design debt tends to need dedicated time and is better assigned to more senior people. Third, human values such as dignity and inclusiveness can be turned into concrete descriptions, which then become requirements, for example about how user information is kept and shared, how users can unsubscribe, or how software supports different languages and cultures.

The takeaways are practical. Teams can use known review smells to plan reviews, set expectations and train novice reviewers. They can use the technical debt findings to decide what to fix and who should fix it, focusing dedicated effort on design debt. And they can translate human values into product requirements to build software responsibly.

talks.title: "Crowd dynamics, RL and Unity: A Journey" by Tomas Diaz
talks.teaser: Models crowd movement with reinforcement learning in Unity, using Kalman filters and recorded pedestrian trajectories as training data.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Tomas Diaz presents a comprehensive exploration of modeling human movement through crowd dynamics, reinforcement learning (RL), and the Unity game engine. The work aims to predict how people navigate shared spaces given desired trajectories, with applications in environmental design, simulation, and behavior analysis. The presentation is divided into four key sections: the historical evolution of crowd dynamics as a field, foundational RL concepts, the Kalman filter for state estimation, and practical implementation in Unity.

## Historical Evolution of Crowd Dynamics
The field emerged from practical engineering needs. In the 1960s, Fruin's work quantified pedestrian sidewalk design using photography to analyze trajectories, introducing the concept of "level of service" (designations A–F based on density and expected flow). The 1970s brought a paradigm shift when Henderson's work demonstrated that Maxwell-Boltzmann mechanics from particle physics could model pedestrian movement, treating people like gaseous particles. The 1990s explosion of computational power enabled simulation-based validation. The social force model emerged as influential, positing that pedestrians are bombarded by attractive and repulsive forces—for instance, a burning wall repels nearby people. Recent research (the "crowd space" paper) revealed that no single algorithm captures all crowd configurations; instead, determining the specific space type and applying the appropriate algorithm yields better results.

## Reinforcement Learning and PPO
Diaz pivots from physics-based models to RL, recognizing that uncovering a hidden universal human motion equation is unlikely. In RL, an agent observes a state from its environment, takes actions, and receives rewards. The policy (π) maps states to action probabilities, parameterized by neural network weights (θ). An advantage function determines whether actions outperformed or underperformed expectations, calculated as discounted cumulative rewards minus expected future rewards. The presentation introduces vanilla policy gradient before focusing on PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization by OpenAI), which prevents destructive policy updates. PPO clamps the ratio of new-to-old policy probabilities within a small range (typically ±0.2 epsilon), ensuring updates remain conservative and preventing the agent from accessing data distributions it was not trained on.

## Kalman Filter and Coleman Gain
Diaz detours to explain Rudolf Kalman's work on optimal state estimation, motivated by Apollo program rocket control. The Kalman filter combines imperfect system equations with noisy sensor readings to estimate true state. The optimal weighting factor—the Kalman gain—minimizes error by dividing system error by the sum of system and sensor error. Matrix formulations account for observation matrices that collapse unmeasured variables (e.g., if only position is sensed, not acceleration). The demonstration with chaotic double pendulums shows how sensor readings "snap" the simulation back toward observed behavior. Ensemble Kalman filtering (running multiple models and averaging) improves tracking. This framework is applied to crowd dynamics: a statistical similarity measure paper uses Kalman filters to quantify how well simulations match real crowd data.

## Unity Implementation
Unity ML-Agents wraps OpenAI's Gym framework, running PyTorch backend with Barracuda inference engine (supporting ONNX format). Developers override methods: OnEpisodeBegin initializes agents and environments, CollectObservations maps environment to state vectors, OnActionReceived applies actions and assigns rewards, and policy configuration specifies PPO hyperparameters. A simple example trains an agent to hit a box by controlling ball forces in x and z coordinates.

## Practical Application and Results
Diaz trains agents on trajectory data from immutable crowds (20–30 trajectories, 2–3 seconds each). Agents receive no explicit reward for reaching destinations; instead, an entropy-based reward metric captures natural crowd behavior. Key insights: (1) sight information (raycasts visualizing nearby agents) is crucial but subject to diminishing returns around 40 rays; (2) reducing information to key dimensions accelerates learning; (3) data augmentation (rotation) and curriculum learning (progressively introducing trajectories) significantly improve performance. Trained agents generalize to unseen environments and different crowd densities without retraining, suggesting they capture underlying behavioral characteristics rather than memorizing trajectories.

## Takeaways
The work demonstrates that RL can extract generalizable crowd behaviors from limited datasets, with potential applications in entertainment and behavioral quantification. Future directions include larger datasets, real-time camera feeds to continuously update training data, and deploying agents for diverse spatial configurations.

talks.title: "Tech When the Sky is Falling: Tools for Crisis Response" by Emma Ferguson and Colin Schimmelfing
talks.teaser: Walks through how a volunteer mask donation project grew from a shared spreadsheet into a real database and tooling stack.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe Mask Match, a peer-to-peer site that ran from March to July 2020 and sent donated masks directly to healthcare workers during the early PPE shortage. It began as a weekend idea after two healthcare startup founders approached the presenters, and it went on to deliver close to a million masks. The talk frames tech-enabled crisis response as five phases: validate the idea, make it repeatable, scale, stabilize, then adapt or shut down.

Each phase came with its own tooling changes. The first version ran on Google Sheets and shared Gmail inboxes, which caused data conflicts and hit concurrency and send limits. The team added a small email app, then Retool for volunteer workflows, a free help-desk tool, Twilio text reminders and eventually Postgres on AWS, with an automatic matcher and Metabase analytics later on. They noted that cleaning data before the Postgres move took weeks, so investing in data quality early would have paid off.

In the final phase, hospital requests tapered off, and large offers of masks arrived that the matching model was not built for. The team chose to shut down gracefully, telling volunteers directly, restricting access and exporting the database before removing it. Their lessons include vetting volunteers, relying on donations and free tiers, and first identifying which phase a project is in before choosing tools.

talks.title: "How Tracing Uncovers Half-truths in Slack’s CI Infrastructure" by Frank Chen
talks.teaser: Shows how distributed tracing helped Slack find the causes of flaky CI tests and cut pull request flake rates.
talks.summary:
Frank Chen, who works on developer productivity at Slack, explains why flaky tests frustrate engineers and erode trust in continuous integration. Slack's CI workflows run for days or weeks and pass through GitHub, Jenkins, Kubernetes and QA environments, so the causes are spread across code, services and people. Conventional logs and metrics struggled to show where failures came from.

The first wins came from tracing the test runner. A prototype trace revealed slow git checkouts on some instances in an autoscaling group that were not being updated. During a multi-day incident, a cross-service trace showed git LFS failures on a third of the QA fleet, and pipelines were flowing again within two hours. A month of instrumenting the Cypress test runtime then linked certain runtime variables to higher flake rates, and roughly 90 hours of large machine time at peak went to tests whose results were discarded.

In an August 2021 incident, back-end unit and integration suites ran out of memory. Per-test-case traces exposed memory jumps across percentiles, and subject matter experts identified suspect experimental pull requests. Reverting one of them made tests appear to pass at a higher rate within minutes. Chen reports that the per-pull-request flake rate fell from about 50 percent to about 5 percent. His takeaway is that tracing with shared context, plus conversations that bring service and test owners together, helps teams find causes faster.

talks.title: "Functional distributed systems beyond request/response" by Melinda Lu
talks.teaser: Explains why event-driven services built on distributed logs can replace synchronous request/response calls between microservices.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the point that any software touching the internet is a distributed system, and that the default way services call each other, synchronous request/response, makes that hard. A network call can be slow, lost or ambiguous, so it is often unclear whether a retry is safe. As service graphs grow, availability and latency compound across dependencies, and teams pile on retries, caches, circuit breakers and service meshes to compensate.

The speaker proposes event-driven services as an alternative, drawing an analogy to functional programming. A producer writes an event to a partitioned log such as Kafka or Kinesis and does not wait for a reply, so consumers can be added or deployed without coordination, and the log buffers work when a consumer is down. A photo-sharing platform was used as a real example: a user following another user fed a feed worker, a push notification pipeline, monitoring and analytics, each as an independent consumer. Two ways of getting database writes into the log were compared, database change capture, which the speaker has used more often, and event sourcing. Machine learning inference was presented as simply another consumer.

The closing section covers the costs. Systems become eventually consistent, ordering guarantees depend on how topics are partitioned, and events need unique identities for deduplication. Schemas should be managed with typed formats such as protocol buffers so they can evolve safely, and deleting a user's data must reach every derived copy. The main takeaway is that event-driven designs need more up-front design but reduce coupling and make later changes simpler, even though tooling and examples are scarcer than for request/response.

talks.title: "Client Side Deep Learning Optimization with PyTorch" by Tyler Kirby and Shane Caldwell
talks.teaser: Shows how to shrink and speed up PyTorch models so they run on phones without a Python runtime.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who build machine learning systems for a moving company, explain why they moved deep learning models from servers onto phones. Server hosting costs money, real-time video needs fast frame rates, and drivers often lack a reliable internet connection. They describe earlier attempts, including a 2017 text classifier written in JavaScript that ran too hot on Android, and an object detector built with TensorFlow Lite that fell short on accuracy. They settled on PyTorch because its eager execution feels like ordinary Python and most published research code uses it.

The middle of the talk walks through the path from an eager module to a deployable one. Models are converted to TorchScript through tracing, scripting, or a mix of both, and the intermediate graph can be inspected before and after optimizations. The serialized model is saved as a .pt file and run from C++ without Python or its global interpreter lock. Practical tips include calling eval mode, warming up the model before timing it, and keeping it cached. The speakers then compare quantization methods: dynamic quantization suits a language-model LSTM, which dropped from 169 MB to 134 MB and from about 5 seconds to 1.6 seconds per batch. Static quantization with per-channel calibration suits a MobileNet, which shrank from 22 MB to 5.6 MB with inference falling from 0.13 to 0.03 seconds and accuracy dropping one point. Quantization-aware training is the fallback when accuracy falls too far.

The closing advice is to choose a mobile-friendly architecture first, serialize to TorchScript, and try quantization before custom optimizations. Track several accuracy metrics so uneven effects on regression and classification are not missed, and stick to operators PyTorch supports on mobile.

talks.title: "The Future of Conferences" by Cristina (Crista) Lopes
talks.teaser: Weighs the value and carbon cost of conferences and what online and hybrid events mean for their future.
talks.summary:
This keynote reflects on where conferences came from, what they are worth, and what they cost. The speaker traces professional and scholarly societies back to the 1300s and notes how their number grew after the printing press. Drawing on decades of attending and organizing events, the speaker says the value of knowledge sharing has fallen as online content has grown, while networking and travel still matter. The costs include time away from family, harassment in crowds, and flight emissions, estimated at around 330 tons of CO2 over twenty years.

A committee within an ACM special interest group studied the carbon footprint of its conferences and found that venues far from North America and Western Europe emitted more. Before the pandemic, the group considered a voluntary carbon tax on registrations. The move online that followed was rapid, and the speaker helped build a virtual conference platform. Recorded videos widened reach and made live Q&A more thoughtful, but time zones, weak social features, and attendees working through what should have been breaks caused problems. The speaker stresses that organizer choices mattered as much as the software. A pre-pandemic virtual community conference was estimated at under a ton of CO2, far below the emissions of travel.

The speaker expects in-person events to return alongside hybrid formats, ranging from one large yearly event plus online gatherings to parallel in-person and online tracks. Technology is not the hard part; social and psychological issues, such as feeling present and being distracted at home, are. The talk closes by asking how to balance unsustainable travel with professionally valuable exchange.

talks.title: "Why security is the biggest benefit of using the Cloud" by AJ Yawn
talks.teaser: Argues that cloud-native controls like AWS Config and service control policies can reduce security risk and speed up response.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security is the most overlooked benefit of cloud computing. The speaker, who runs a compliance automation company, notes that cloud pitches focus on cost, elasticity and scalability while rarely mentioning security. Security and speed are not opposing forces when controls start early in the pipeline. Core ideas such as protecting identities, knowing the perimeter and responding to vulnerabilities apply wherever workloads run. Simply lifting servers into the cloud keeps old habits, while re-architecting around cloud-native services opens up better options. Under the shared responsibility model, the provider secures the underlying infrastructure, while customers remain responsible for access, data placement and what users can do.

A live demo showed AWS Config checking a newly created S3 bucket for encryption and public access. The rule automatically remediated the bucket and sent a Slack notification, shortening the time between detection and response without waking an engineer. For account structure, the speaker recommended AWS Organizations to split workloads so that a compromised user account holding no resources has little to reach. Service control policies then restricted allowed regions and blocked disabling of security services. The demo showed that even an administrator was denied an EC2 call in a region outside the allowed list.

The closing argument is that teams should automate repetitive security checks so people can focus on proactive threat hunting. Security should be involved early in projects, and overlapping compliance frameworks can be handled through shared controls. The speaker also urged attendees to consider how tools affect people's quality of life and to widen hiring pools.

talks.title: "Asami: Turn your JSON into a Graph in 2 Lines" by Paula Gearon
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Asami: Turn your JSON into a Graph in 2 Lines" by Paula Gearon.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Paula Gearon, a Technical Leader at Cisco Systems, introduces Asami, an open-source graph database developed in Clojure and ClojureScript. Gearon details the background and motivations behind Asami's creation, the mathematical foundations of graph databases, and how Asami's storage and indexing architecture enables fast in-memory and durable querying. She highlights how Asami handles flexible, schema-less JSON imports in just two lines of code and shares real-world use cases, including integration into Cisco's SecureX security product and inspecting complex network packet capture files.

### Key Topics
- **Origins and Requirements**: Developing an open-source, Clojure-based graph database to run in both backend systems and web browsers via ClojureScript, evolving from in-memory pattern matching to a Datomic-style graph database with aggregates.
- **Graph Theory and Data Modeling**: Representing entities and relations as directed edges and nodes (statements/triples). Unlike systems that strictly distinguish attributes from edges, Asami maps attributes as edges and values as nodes.
- **Triple Indexing and Nested Maps**: Organizing graph statements across three column orderings to enable rapid lookups, pattern rewriting, and joins without full table scans, leveraging Clojure's immutable data structures.
- **Durability and Copy-on-Write Trees**: Storing statements as numeric tuples (up to 512 elements per array block) organized in tree indexes (such as AVL trees) using copy-on-write semantics and memory-mapped files.
- **Time-Travel and Immutability**: Tracking root node snapshots with timestamps and transaction IDs to support querying historic database states without altering committed data.
- **JSON Ingestion and Ad-Hoc Analysis**: Loading raw, untyped JSON directly using string attributes and querying unstructured keys and values using a GraalVM-compiled command-line interface.

### Technical Details
- **Compact In-Memory and Durable Encodings**: Values fitting within 60 bits (short strings, keywords, booleans, timestamps, and numbers) are packed into a 64-bit integer, using high-order bits for type tags and lengths. Data exceeding 8 bytes is serialized into buffers referenced by byte offsets and indexed with trees storing the first 16 bytes per node.
- **Layered Protocols**: Architecture separated cleanly via Clojure protocols, allowing the block graph to swap underlying implementations (e.g., tuple storage, AVL trees, and memory-mapped block buffers) without altering higher layers.
- **Pattern Rewriting vs. Hash Joins**: Asami evaluates query patterns through iterative pattern rewriting and indexed lookups, providing fast join execution.
- **Transitive Closures & Optimization**: Implementation of Sparkle-inspired transitive closures uses self-doubling steps (reaching 256 steps in 8 iterations), reducing linear query times from 90 seconds to roughly 80 milliseconds.
- **CLI & GraalVM**: Compiled to a native command-line tool, enabling analysts to ingest large files (such as a 7 MB packet capture JSON), index them, and query regex-matched attributes (like query keys containing spaces) within seconds.

### Takeaways
Asami offers a lightweight (~7,000 lines of Clojure vs. 100,000 lines of Java in older systems like Mulgara), schema-agnostic solution for loading arbitrary JSON directly into an indexed graph. While bulk indexing large multi-gigabyte datasets requires time, lazy loading and copy-on-write storage deliver sub-second query performance and time-travel querying. It is actively deployed at Cisco in security tooling such as SecureX.

talks.title: "How Flutter Can Change the Future of Urban Communities" by Edward Thornton
talks.teaser: Shows how the cross-platform Flutter toolkit speeds up building community safety apps and startup MVPs across devices.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software developer, opens with a community safety app he built after the Ferguson unrest in St. Louis. Users post local incidents, which then appear as clustered markers on a map so residents can see where problems have been reported. He demonstrates adding posts live, and says the app was later used in Nigeria during protests over police brutality to coordinate and share information.

He then introduces Flutter, an open-source toolkit launched by Google in 2017 that compiles one codebase to Android, iOS, Linux, Windows and the web. It has two parts: an SDK with tools for building and compiling, and a widget-based user interface framework. He argues its main strengths are fast development, shown through hot reload as he changes a name and a color and sees the result immediately, a single codebase, customizable widgets, and easy adaptation to different screen sizes. He also covers lower development cost for startups building minimum viable products, plus a large community and learning resources.

He closes by showing FlutterFlow, a tool that speeds up mobile app creation further, and points to a map of countries where Flutter is gaining adoption, including Brazil, Puerto Rico and parts of Africa and the Middle East. His takeaway is that Flutter suits fast-moving urban communities and is a good starting point for beginners. He notes that its web support is still maturing.

talks.title: "Nim Nuggets: Systems Programming & Metaprogramming Magic" by Aditya Siram
talks.teaser: Shows Nim's compile-time introspection, destructor-based memory management, and C++ interop through live code demos.
talks.summary:
Aditya Siram introduces Nim, a statically typed imperative language that blends ideas from Ada, Modula, Oberon, Pascal and Lisp and compiles through C. He opens with a small web server that returns a capitalised URL path as JSON, then shows C-style manual allocation and freeing, and explains uniform function call syntax, which lets ordinary functions be chained with dot notation. He argues that fast compile times matter most for developer feedback, citing a full bootstrap of a few minutes on an old laptop.

The middle of the talk covers static introspection. Code runs at compile time through an interpreter, the compiler can report whether an expression compiles and what type it has, and a macro diffs two versions of a Person type to generate a migration type. A second example shows that a migration needing a real transformation, such as turning a string address into a structured one, must be supplied explicitly. Static resource management follows: destructors are injected after a value's last use, and a consumed value that is used again gets destroyed twice until a copy hook is marked as an error, at which point the compiler reports the conflict.

The final section covers C++ interop, mapping Nim types to std::vector and unique_ptr with templates and reusing them without leaks, plus a compile-time factorial built on a recursive template trick. The takeaway is that fast feedback, introspection, controllable memory management, and C++ interop make Nim practical in places where few languages fit.

talks.title: "Game Development in Eight Bits" by Kevin Zurawel
talks.teaser: Explains how the NES handled graphics, physics, random numbers and saves within its tight hardware limits.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through the Nintendo Entertainment System, a 1985 console built around a 6502 processor with 2 KB of system RAM, 2 KB of video RAM and no operating system or clock. Kevin Zurawel shows how developers worked within those limits. Backgrounds were built from 8x8 tiles stored as grid references, sprites were capped at 64 on screen, and Super Mario Bros. fit a 14-screen level into about 101 bytes by reusing repeated scenery.

Physics and collision needed similar shortcuts. Mario's weighted movement came from fixed-point numbers that track sub-pixel positions, since the processor could only add, subtract and shift. Contra treated the player as a single point tested against a rectangle that shifted with the player's pose. For random numbers, Tetris used a shift register, Final Fantasy stepped through a hard-coded table of 256 values, and Contra mixed the frame counter into a byte.

Saving was the last hurdle. Early games relied on passwords, and the Famicom Disk System offered writable disks that were easy to copy, so cartridges with battery-backed RAM followed. Holding reset while powering off protected save data from a processor that can misbehave as power fades, and Dragon Warrior kept several checksummed copies of its save. The takeaway is that a simple, shippable fix often beats a perfect one until it proves inadequate.

talks.title: "Whoops! I Rewrote it in Rust" by Brian Martin
talks.teaser: Follows a Twitter engineer's effort to rewrite a memcache-compatible cache server and its storage layer in Rust without losing speed.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software engineer at Twitter, explains that the company's Pelican caching framework, written in C and used to maintain forks of memcache and Redis, needed TLS support. The team wanted to add it in Rust without giving up the throughput and tail latency of the C version. An earlier 2019 Rust server built on the Tokio runtime ran about 10 to 15 percent slower in throughput and 25 to 30 percent higher at p99.9, which was not acceptable for production. Tail latency matters because a large fan-out makes it likely that a user-facing request hits a slow cache response.

To isolate the problem, the speaker rebuilt a minimal ping server on mio, a thin wrapper over epoll, with TLS provided by BoringSSL, and it matched the C benchmarks. A cache server followed, using the standard hash map as a stand-in for storage. The C storage library was tied into the metrics and logging frameworks, so the speaker rewrote it in Rust as a single-threaded segment design. Segments group items by expiry time rather than by size, which allows efficient expiry, new eviction strategies, and about five bytes of metadata per item instead of 39 in the slab design. The Rust cache server beat upstream memcache at high throughput, and persistent memory storage retained about 93 percent of DRAM performance in a 4:1 read-write test.

The rewrite took about two months and duplicated earlier design work, and feature parity was still incomplete. Tools such as cargo bench, cargo fuzz, and clippy helped with micro-benchmarking, protocol fuzzing, and code quality, and an all-Rust build was easier to maintain than CMake. Remaining work includes finishing features, canary testing, multi-threaded tuning, and building a Redis replacement.

talks.title: "Type-Driven API Design in Rust" by Will Crichton
talks.teaser: Shows how Rust traits and type-state can make a progress bar API that catches misuse at compile time.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from tqdm, a Python utility that wraps any iterable to show a progress bar with minimal code. The speaker points out its rough edges: a wrongly typed argument only fails at runtime, and some option combinations quietly show nothing, such as a custom bar format applied to an unbounded counter. Using that API as the target, the speaker builds a comparable progress bar in Rust, one step at a time.

Starting from a concrete loop, the design is generalized over the element type and then over any iterable, using generics bounded by the standard Iterator trait. A progress struct wraps an iterator so callers can use the same wrapping style as tqdm. An extension trait then adds a method to every iterator type, including types the author does not own. For bounded iterators, the ExactSizeIterator trait unlocks a method that draws a bar with a length, and calling it on an unbounded range fails at compile time. Finally, a type-state pattern encodes bounded versus unbounded in the type itself, so the delimiter-setting method exists only in the bounded state and misuse becomes a compile error.

The main takeaways are that traits are the central unit for organizing a Rust API, that they allow extending types you do not own, and that where clauses and type states can move misuse checks from documentation or runtime into the compiler. The speaker also notes the trade-off: compiler errors can be verbose and hard to read, so designers must weigh them against clearer runtime errors.

talks.title: "Prevent Phishing & Impersonation" by Karissa McKelvey
talks.teaser: Proposes a relationship-based identity system that replaces self-announced profiles with one-time invitation codes and local names.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how social engineering unfolds: attackers map relationships between users and businesses, impersonate a trusted party, pull personal details, and then escalate to exploits or ransomware. Most defenses target infrastructure, key verification and phishing training, but the speaker argues the weak point is self-announced user profiles that anyone can copy and that depend on a third party to validate them. Examples include iMessage's name suggestions, which bring back spoofable lookups, and Keybase-style social proofs, where the recipient still has to check who is genuine.

The speaker presents Back Channel, a prototype built around relationships instead of global namespaces. Two people exchange a one-time numeric code that expires after about a minute; both apps derive a shared secret from it and open an end-to-end encrypted channel, with the relay treated as untrusted and swappable. Each person names the other in a local contact list that never leaves the device. Multi-device linking uses QR codes and CRDT-based syncing, and a lost device can be revoked with a tombstone message that wipes its data. Demos cover chat and document review sharing.

User tests with journalists, researchers and designers showed that most participants did not notice they never created an account. Known gaps include a single relay as an availability risk, unresolved revocation edge cases, no key rotation, and no storage peer, so messages only sync when both people are online. Group invitations and enterprise uses, such as exchanging a code with a supervisor during a video call, were left as open questions.

talks.title: "Simple Made Easy"
talks.teaser: Argues that simplicity means unentangled parts rather than familiarity, and shows how complecting drives software complexity.
talks.summary:
Rich Hickey argues that developers often confuse "simple" with "easy" and pay too little attention to the entanglement that makes software hard to understand and change. He traces the origins of both words: simple refers to a single fold or braid, meaning unentangled, while easy is relative, tied to what is nearby or familiar to a particular person. He defines complexity as complecting, the braiding together of concerns such as state and identity, inheritance and types, or rules scattered through code.

He argues that reliability depends on being able to reason about a program, and that type checkers and test suites act as guard rails rather than direction. Chasing ease from the start, he says, is like a sprinter running flat out from the first step of a long race. He offers simpler alternatives: immutable values, plain functions, maps and sets for data, queues to decouple components, declarative rules, and protocols for polymorphism. Simple tools, he notes, can build the same sophisticated systems.

Simplicity is a choice that takes deliberate effort, and it concerns the resulting artifact rather than how code is typed. Many small separate components can be simpler than a few tangled ones. The talk closes by urging developers to build a sensitivity to entanglement so they can argue for simpler designs with colleagues.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Paula Gearon about the Asami graph database
talks.teaser: Explains Asami, an open-source graph database written in Clojure for JVM and browser use, and how it handles queries and storage.
talks.summary:
Asami is an open-source graph database written in Clojure, maintained by an engineer at Cisco's Threat Grid group. In this interview, the maintainer explains that it started as an in-memory store for an internal rules engine, built so the team would not depend on a commercial system. As the storage layer grew, it became its own project. It now runs on the JVM and in the browser through ClojureScript, and durable on-disk storage is being finished ahead of a 2.0 release.

The discussion covers the data model, where nodes and labelled, directed edges represent entities and the relationships between them. The query language combines the Datomic-style EDN syntax with SPARQL semantics, so most queries written for Datomic or DataScript can be reused, though edge cases such as negation and certain unions follow SPARQL behaviour. Asami is tuned for querying and analysis over data gathered from many sources, at the cost of slower loading when writes are frequent. Because stored data is immutable, replication across a cluster is comparatively simple, and the history of earlier values is kept and can be queried.

The maintainer closes by pointing listeners to the project's GitHub repository under the threadgrid organisation, its online documentation, and the #asami channel on the Clojurians Slack. The takeaway is that Asami suits Clojure developers who need to link disparate data and run many analytical queries over it.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Joel Holdbrooks about Meander
talks.teaser: Explains how the Clojure pattern-matching library Meander supports rewriting data, and where its next release is headed.
talks.summary:
Joel Holdbrooks, creator of the Clojure library Meander, sits down for a conversation about how the project started and where it is going. He traces his motivation to everyday programming, where code often pulls data apart one way and rebuilds it another. That asymmetry struck him as odd compared with how equations are handled in mathematics. Rewriting systems, which turn one arrangement of symbols into another, offered a model he wanted to bring into Clojure.

The discussion walks newcomers through pattern matching, starting with regular expressions and the destructuring found in mainstream languages. Placeholders bind to parts of a structure, and rewriting applies those bindings to a new shape on the right-hand side. Joel describes his goal of symmetry, where anything expressible on the left of a rule can also appear on the right. He explains that an unbound logic variable causes substitution to fail, a choice made after users reported that the earlier restriction on disjunctions was a pain point. Meander also runs in ClojureScript, where it can match on JavaScript objects and arrays, and it can be extended with new behaviour.

On performance, he says users report slow patterns, and the team has closed much of the gap with handwritten code, sometimes beating it through dead code elimination and inference. The next version aims to add an interpreter, quoted patterns, macros, explanations for why a match fails, and a unified framework, with a release targeted before the end of the year.

talks.title: "Systems that run forever self-heal and scale" by Joe Armstrong (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how isolated processes, message passing and supervision let long-running systems survive crashes and scale.
talks.summary:
Joe Armstrong opens with the goal of building systems that keep running for years, recover from crashes and grow to very large size. He argues that distributed programming is hard mainly because of data consistency and failure handling, while running many small isolated processes that exchange messages is comparatively easy. Using a hash-based placement scheme, he shows how a piece of data can be located across a cluster of machines, then explains why replicating data across just two machines leaves the system in an uncertain state after a crash. Leader election in Paxos-style protocols, he notes, is notoriously difficult to get right.

The core of the talk is a set of six rules for fault-tolerant systems: isolation, concurrency, failure detection, fault identification, live code upgrade and stable storage. Armstrong argues that isolation brings fault tolerance, scalability, testability and upgradability together, and that a failing process should be allowed to crash rather than be defended against. Linked processes and supervising workers then restart what has failed. He describes Erlang's lightweight processes, asynchronous message passing and OTP design principles, and reports that well-structured programs speed up on multi-core machines without code changes.

He points to production uses such as Ericsson telephony base station software, CouchDB, RabbitMQ and a Chef server monitoring large numbers of machines. A live profiler demo shows bottlenecks where many worker processes funnel into one central process. He closes by urging developers to reason about the collective behaviour of very large numbers of processes rather than individual ones.

talks.title: "Swearjure" by Gary Fredericks (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how to write Clojure programs using only non-alphanumeric characters, and what that subset can and cannot express.
talks.summary:
Gary Fredericks presents Swearjure, an esoteric subset of Clojure whose programs contain no alphanumeric characters. The work is led by Tim McCormick and John Nicholas Laronge. He starts with what can be expressed: any positive integer, built by adding ones obtained from a multiplication call with no arguments; negative numbers and ratios through the negation and division functions; true and false through equality checks; and nil by looking up a missing key in an empty map. Floats remain out of reach.

Data structures are built mainly with the backtick reader, using unquote and unquote-splicing to cons onto lists, concatenate sequences, and make vectors. Functions can only be written with the reader literal, and it cannot be nested, so the talk shows workarounds such as wrapping a value in a vector and immediately calling it to return a data structure. Control flow relies on a function table, a map of functions passed as the first argument, which simulates if and recursion but consumes stack on every call.

On limits, he notes that Swearjure lacks Java interop, floats and higher-order features, so it is not Clojure complete and is not clearly Turing complete, though he believes the SKI calculus could be implemented. He concludes it is largely impractical yet surprisingly capable, and invites people to try it in production, report results, and help find ways to get changes into Clojure that would make it more powerful.

talks.title: "Babel: An Untyped, Stack-based HLL" by Clayton Bauman (2013)
talks.teaser: Walks through a stack-based, untyped language with built-in security primitives and a live demo of its interpreter.
talks.summary:
Clayton Bauman, the author of the Babel programming language, opens by arguing that device security depends on who controls the software a device runs. He ties the recent surveillance revelations to proprietary hardware, digital rights restrictions and government backdoors, and argues that the focus should shift toward the rights of device owners. Babel 1.0 is planned to use public key cryptography so the interpreter can check whether a piece of code is allowed to run locally. He is clear that this does not fix an insecure underlying platform.

He then introduces the language itself: a general-purpose, untyped, stack-based language in postfix order, with optional type tags. Data lives in leaf arrays, pointers in interior arrays, and tagged pointers carry a 128-bit hash. The virtual machine uses a data stack, an up stack and a managed return stack, along with a symbol table and a bootstrap written in Babel itself. The reference implementation is written in C, with a Perl front end that compiles S-expression source into bytecode.

The live demo covers hello world, arithmetic, iterating over lists and random numbers, hash table lookups, loops, and the difference between dupe and copy. He also shows unload and load to serialize a structure to a file and read it back, and reads environment variables through the symbol table. The talk ends with a program that loads and runs compiled Babel code from a file. He closes by noting that the language is still in development, with more crypto primitives, compression, web access and cross-platform builds planned.
