talks.title: "Nimrod: A new approach to meta programming" by Andreas Rumpf (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how Nim's macros, templates and term rewriting rules move work to compile time, using a hello world program as the example.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who designed the Nim language (called Nimrod in the talk), introduces it as a compiled language that generates C, JavaScript, C++ and Objective-C code and includes a real-time garbage collector. He explains how a hello world program works, including overloaded dollar conversions for custom types, and how a macro can derive a not-equals operator from a user's equals operator.

The core of the talk demonstrates macros on small examples. A tag macro generates HTML helper procedures, an immediate macro avoids type inference on undeclared names, and a once template runs a block exactly once using a hygienic guard. Lazy templates delay the evaluation of logging arguments, and an HTML domain-specific language is expanded into a procedure that the compiler evaluates at compile time into one string literal. Term rewriting macros then optimize a format operator by partially evaluating literal format strings, and a regex example hoists repeated pattern construction out of a loop.

The closing recap notes that compile-time evaluation, declarative and imperative AST macros, and term rewriting all help move work out of runtime. Term rewriting rules can be tricky and buggy, so they carry names that allow them to be disabled. Static file reading, external process execution, custom pragmas and quasi-quoting were mentioned but not demonstrated. The main takeaway is that macros let library authors optimize code without changing how it is written.

talks.title: "Enso: Composing DSL Interpreters, Languages & Aspects" by William Cook (2013)
talks.teaser: Presents Enso, a system for writing executable models and interpreted DSLs that compose into full applications without glue code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that developers carry an implicit strategy for building software. That strategy shapes all the code they write, yet it is rarely written down, so changing it later is costly. William Cook proposes making the strategy explicit by describing an application as a model and running that model through strategies implemented as interpreters or meta-programs. He contrasts this with the common practice of using small domain-specific languages embedded in a larger program and joined by general-purpose glue code.

Cook walks through examples built in Enso. A data manager turns schema-style descriptions into objects with checked fields, and optional behaviours such as mutability rules, observation, security checks and persistence can be selected across all data. Grammars are bidirectional, can build graphs rather than only trees, and are interpreted directly without parser or code generation. Four self-describing root schemas anchor the system, and a stencil maps a schema onto an editable diagram that stays synchronised with the underlying model. He also described a heating-system case from a language workbench challenge, where a state-machine controller and an asynchronous simulator updated the models live.

Cook is candid that Enso is currently slow but usable, and that partial evaluation is the planned route to better performance. The takeaway is that developers should make their designs executable and programmable, so that changing a strategy changes the resulting system's behaviour.

talks.title: "zip Code: Unpacking Data Compression" by Scott Vokes (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains core lossless compression algorithms and how a compressor was built to fit tiny embedded devices.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why data compression matters beyond file archives, pointing to gzip on web traffic, zip and tarball packaging, and streaming audio and video. Compression is framed as detecting and removing duplication in data, with the shortest possible description of a pattern as the goal. The speaker focuses on lossless methods, while lossy codecs such as JPEG get a shorter look near the end.

The core algorithms are covered in rough order of complexity. Run-length coding replaces repeated symbols with counts, and delta coding stores small gaps between sorted numbers. Huffman coding assigns short bit patterns to frequent tokens based on their statistics. The LZ77 sliding window and LZ78 dictionary methods replace repeated sequences with back references, with LZSS and LZW as variants, and DEFLATE combines these ideas with Huffman coding. The Burrows-Wheeler transform reorders data so that similar characters group together, which is the basis of bzip2.

The main case study is Heat Shrink, an LZSS library written for microcontrollers with only a few kilobytes of RAM. Decompression needs under 50 bytes and compression about 100 bytes, and the library is built as a state machine so input and output can be processed incrementally without blocking real-time tasks. A bug in handling 12-bit offsets surfaced before release and was fixed by splitting one state. The practical takeaway is to benchmark on representative data and to structure formats so they compress well.

talks.teaser: Shows how software engineering methods can design and simulate DNA circuits and cell behaviour before any lab work.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software engineering practices, such as abstraction, formal methods and simulation, could help biologists design living systems more reliably. It starts with DNA as a programmable medium, explaining base pairing and strand displacement, where a short toehold lets one strand push another off a longer duplex. Those reactions can be composed into logic gates such as AND and OR.

The speaker demonstrates a design tool that takes named strand components and compiles a circuit into the full set of intermediate species. Deterministic and stochastic simulations then show whether a design should behave as intended before anything is built in a lab. A three-component oscillator is solved against a parts database, and a poor candidate is contrasted with a better one that oscillates despite noise. Other examples include an approximate majority circuit and a square root circuit, which a collaborator checked with an SMT solver.

The talk then moves up to cells, comparing their parallelism and energy efficiency with current computers. It notes that DNA reading and writing costs are falling faster than Moore's law, although writing DNA remains expensive. A synthetic biology company's antimalarial precursor is cited as an example of engineered cells in production, and a GPU-based simulation of biofilm colony growth closes the talk. The takeaway is that simulation-first design could make biological engineering more predictable, though simulation parameters are not yet accurate enough for precise predictions.

talks.title: "Learnfun and Playfun: A Nintendo automation system" by Tom Murphy VII (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how two programs learn winning criteria from NES memory and then play old games automatically.
talks.summary:
Tom Murphy VII presents Learnfun and Playfun, two programs that play old Nintendo Entertainment System games without being taught the rules. The goal is a general, deliberately absurd method rather than skilled play. The NES suits this because its tiny memory keeps game state, such as position, world, level and coin count, at fixed addresses that a program can read directly.

Learnfun watches a recording of a person playing and examines memory snapshot by snapshot. It searches for ordered combinations of memory locations that tend to increase as progress is made, then assigns weights to them. Playfun uses these weighted objectives to choose button presses. Brute force is hopeless given the size of the input space and the cost of emulating each step, so it generates random futures about five seconds long, tests short sets of next inputs by the best outcome they can reach, scores the futures, keeps the promising ones and mutates them. Its random inputs follow the speaker's own button habits, and the search is spread across several machines over a network connection.

The closing section covers both successful runs and comically failed ones, such as jumping into pits. The practical takeaway is that a program can derive a progress signal from raw memory alone, without knowing the game's rules. That approach depends on being able to emulate the system and save and reload its states, which limits how far it applies to most real-world targets.

talks.title: "Xiki: GUI and Text Interfaces are Converging" by Craig Muth (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how a plain-text outline language can render one set of nested menus as web, command-line, desktop, and voice interfaces.
talks.summary:
Craig Muth presents Xiki, a lightweight user interface language built around nested menus. He argues that a simple UI should need little more than an indented outline in one plain-text file, and he shows the same outline rendered as a mobile menu, a web page, a command-line menu, a desktop window, and a voice prompt. The talk starts with a flight-booking example that grows from a few items into a menu with headings, inline Ruby code, and URL-style paths.

The middle of the talk focuses on developer uses. A trailing slash makes a line behave like a directory, and plain-text records can be edited inline and saved back to a SQL table. A text editor plugin runs a line when it is double-clicked and places the output beneath it. Further examples include shell commands, directory trees, code search, Rails console access, Bootstrap and DOM editing, and note-taking with memorization mode. A Rails plugin lets end users add menus to an app by visiting URLs that do not yet exist.

In closing, Craig compares GUI and text tooling. He notes that end-user software has largely moved to graphical interfaces while developer tools remain text-based, and he predicts that voice interfaces will make textual conversation with users more important. He invites developers to try Xiki, to support the project, and to pair with him on its development.

talks.title: "A Relational Exploration of the Chomsky Hierarchy" by Daniel Friedman and William Byrd (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how relational programming with miniKanren can run automata, quines and combinator logic in both directions.
talks.summary:
Friedman and Byrd open with a review of miniKanren, a relational language embedded in Scheme. They walk through run, fresh, equality, disequality, and the type constraints symbolo and numbero, then absento, which forbids one term from appearing anywhere inside another. They explain how eigen variables stand in for arbitrary values that can be stored or compared but not inspected, and how query variables are reported back as answers.

The middle of the talk moves to finite automata. Using a nondeterministic automaton from Sipser's textbook, they encode it directly as mutually recursive relations instead of converting it to a deterministic machine, whose state count can grow sharply. The same definition can accept strings or, run in reverse, generate accepted strings. A test checks the nondeterministic version against a deterministic one by confirming that generated answers match. They then extend the approach to a pushdown automaton by representing its stack as a list. Quines are shown next, followed by a short demonstration that generates many "I love you" programs.

The final section covers combinatory logic, with the S, K, I and W combinators and their reduction rules, plus a relational reducer for combinator terms. A search for a Y combinator is slow, so the speakers supply a hint about a self-applying form, which produces a fixed-point combinator. Because Scheme is call-by-value, they replace it with the Z combinator and compute factorial, returning 120. The takeaway is that a relational definition can run in both directions, so one program can both check and produce the objects it describes.

talks.title: "Add ALL the things: abstract algebra meets analytics" by Avi Bryant (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how monoids from abstract algebra let analytics systems roll up counts, maxes, averages and estimates across many machines.
talks.summary:
Avi Bryant opens with a statsd-style metrics pipeline in which a stream of payment amounts is folded into a running total. Addition works well here for three reasons: a single value is enough to hold, partial totals from separate time buckets or machines can be combined in any order or grouping, and only small results need to cross the network. He shows that taking a maximum has the same properties, which leads to the idea of a commutative monoid: a set, an associative and commutative operation, and an identity element.

He then fits several other aggregations into this shape. Top-k lists merge by combining two lists and keeping the largest entries. Averages carry a running sum and count and divide only when the result is presented. Histograms are element-wise sums of bucketed vectors. For unique counts, each item is hashed to a point between zero and one and the minimum of many hashes is kept, giving a HyperLogLog-style estimate in bounded space. For frequency, he uses a count-min sketch, a matrix of counters with one hash function per row, where a query takes the minimum across the rows. He notes that a plain min is not a clean fit because zero is not its identity.

He distinguishes monoids from groups, which also have inverses. Sums and counts can absorb a refund by adding a negative value, but unique counts cannot be rolled back. The structures also compose, such as a count-min sketch whose cells hold HyperLogLog counters. For practitioners, he points to Twitter's Algebra library in Scala as the main open-source reference, along with a blog that explains and simulates these probabilistic methods.

talks.title: "Programming a 144-computer chip to minimize power"
talks.teaser: Shows how a 144-processor chip is programmed in Forth to cut energy use per instruction.
talks.summary:
Chuck Moore introduces the Forth language and GreenArrays' 144-computer chip, a small die in which each computer talks to its neighbors. He argues that energy per operation should matter more than speed or size when writing software, since future devices such as wearables and sensors will have little power and memory. Each node has 64 words of RAM, two stacks and four ports to adjacent nodes, and its instruction set is small enough that source code maps almost directly onto machine code.

He then walks through example code. Communication between neighbors is a blocking handshake, so a node waiting for data draws almost no power. One demonstration drives an external ceramic oscillator from a single pin, waking the node only on signal edges and letting the oscillation ring down between pulses. Other examples show how preloaded stack values replace literal fetches, how circular stacks let a neighbor supply data endlessly, and why a repeated single instruction in a loop costs less energy than alternating between two.

He closes with practical guidance. Measure power with a meter on the supply, keep stacks and loops free of random data because switching bits costs energy, and prefer jumps within the same memory page. The most important step is reducing the number of instructions executed, which usually means choosing a better algorithm. Placing active nodes near the I/O pins and minimizing the hops that messages take between nodes also reduces waste.

talks.title: "Raft - The Understandable Distributed Protocol" by Ben Johnson (2013)
talks.teaser: Walks through the Raft consensus protocol, covering leader election, log replication and network partitions.
talks.summary:
The talk explains distributed consensus, the problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value or system state. Typical uses include replicated databases, leader election and distributed locks. After a brief outline of Paxos and its many roles, the speaker introduces Raft as an easier-to-understand alternative built around three roles: leader, follower and candidate.

Leader election is walked through step by step. Followers that stop hearing from a leader wait a randomized timeout, become candidates in a new term and win with a majority of votes. Split votes can stall an election until a later term resolves it. Once elected, the leader replicates log entries to followers and commits an entry when a majority has stored it, with heartbeats carrying the commit status.

Network partitions are the hard case. A cut-off leader can accept writes that never reach a majority, while the other side elects a new leader and commits its own values. When the partition heals, the stale leader steps down and rolls back its uncommitted entries. The talk closes with unbounded log growth and slow recovery, and three snapshot strategies from the accompanying paper. The main takeaway is that a majority must stay reachable and that one leader per term keeps state consistent.

talks.title: "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted" by Martha Girdler (2013)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted" by Martha Girdler (2013).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted," Martha Girdler, a software engineer at Uber, breaks down the internal mechanics of how ECMAScript specifications dictate JavaScript code execution. Rather than diving into low-level compiler construction or bytecode emission, Girdler examines how JavaScript engines manage language complexity through execution contexts, the variable object lifecycle, scoping rules, and context binding.

### Key Topics
- **Compilation vs. Interpretation**: While JavaScript source code is traditionally parsed into an abstract syntax tree (AST), bytecode, and interpreted into machine code, modern engines like V8 optimize execution by translating directly into machine code.
- **Function Lifecycle and Execution Phases**: Because functions are first-class objects in JavaScript, comprehending function creation versus execution is fundamental. Function creation sets up scope and context before code execution actually runs.
- **Execution Contexts & The Call Stack**: JavaScript operates in a single-threaded runtime where execution contexts are queued in a call stack. The three main context types are Global, Function, and Eval (with Eval noted as dangerous and excluded from common practice). Contexts are pushed when functions are called and popped upon completion.
- **Variable Objects and Hoisting**: During the creation phase of an execution context, an internal variable object is populated with argument parameters, function declarations (pointers stored immediately), and variable declarations (initialized as `undefined`). Hoisting explains why referencing variables prior to their declaration returns `undefined` rather than throwing a `ReferenceError`.
- **Scope Chain vs. Block Scoping**: JavaScript relies on function-level and global-level scoping rather than block-level scoping. Identifiers resolve sequentially upwards through parent variable objects to the global object.
- **Context Binding (`this`)**: Unlike identifiers resolved through lexical scope, `this` is a keyword referencing the object to which the function is applied during invocation (e.g., top-level functions defaulting to the global `window` object, method calls binding to the receiving object, and constructors pointing to the newly generated instance).
- **Closures**: Closures form naturally when a function retains access to the variable object and scope chain present at its creation, allowing internal data encapsulation.

### Technical Details
Girdler demonstrates the distinction between identifier resolution and keyword binding using code examples featuring custom objects (`bee` and `puppycat`). She highlights that assigning a method defined on one object to a property on another rebinds `this` to whichever object currently invokes the method. Additionally, she presents a "Find the Kitten" example illustrating how a closure encapsulates private state within an outer function scope while returning an interface method capable of operating on that hidden variable.

### Takeaways
Developers can demystify JavaScript's counterintuitive quirks by analyzing ECMAScript internal behaviors. Recognizing the two-stage lifecycle—creation (where hoisting, variable objects, and scope chains are established) and execution (where assignments take place and `this` is evaluated)—provides a predictable mental model for debugging hoisting, variable resolution, and context bugs.

talks.title: "Web Apps in Clojure and ClojureScript with Pedestal" by Brenton Ashworth (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how the Pedestal ClojureScript library structures large interactive browser apps with messages, data flow and web workers.
talks.summary:
Brenton Ashworth argues that interactive applications, which need a continuous two-way flow of information, move coordination work into the browser. These long-running apps grow large, so they need real engineering structure to stay responsive. He presents Pedestal, a client-side ClojureScript library, as a functional alternative to libraries that rely on mutation and object-oriented patterns.

To ground the discussion, he describes a sales funnel visualization built for a client. Events arrived from collectors and a queue, were processed by aggregators into Datomic, and an analyzer sent browser updates about twice a second. Drawing was handled by JavaScript widgets built on Raphael and Highcharts, which held no application state. Pedestal managed the state and logic. A live demo compared two runs of the same code: one stalled while processing updates on the main thread, while the other ran the application logic in a web worker and stayed smooth.

The talk explains the core ideas: separating rendering, services and application logic, passing messages over queues rather than making direct calls, and keeping state in a tree with path-based change reporting. Data flow recomputes functions only when their inputs change, which makes dependencies explicit and logic easy to test. The speaker closed with planned changes, including core.async channels, separate inform and transform messages, and fixed-point data flow. The main takeaway is to keep application logic pure and isolated from rendering and back-end communication.

talks.title: "Native Speed on the Web: JavaScript and asm.js" by Alon Zakai (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how JavaScript can approach native speed in browsers using asm.js, typed arrays, and proposed SIMD and threading features.
talks.summary:
Alon Zakai presents evidence that native applications can run on the web at near-native speeds through JavaScript and asm.js. He demonstrates the Epic Citadel demo—the Unreal Engine 3 compiled from approximately one million lines of C++ to JavaScript—running in browsers at 58–60 frames per second without plugins. Over six months, the same demo improved from 20-second startup and 40 fps to 10-second startup and 60 fps, driven by browser optimization.

The talk introduces asm.js, a formally defined subset of JavaScript designed for optimization. Key features include typed arrays for data representation, bitwise operations (e.g., x|0) to enforce 32-bit integer types, and closure captures to provide static guarantees that variables never change. These patterns emerged naturally across multiple C++ to JavaScript compilers (Emscripten, Mandreel) before being standardized.

Benchmark results show asm.js code running 0.5–2× slower than native C++ equivalents. Box2D physics engine comparisons reveal asm.js outperforming standard JavaScript across Firefox, Chrome, and Internet Explorer 10. Firefox and Chrome achieve speeds comparable to Java, while Safari shows weaker typed array optimization and Internet Explorer is improving.

Three principal challenges remain to achieve full native speed: (1) 32-bit floating point support—JavaScript uses 64-bit doubles, with potential 10–20% speedup from 32-bit floats; ES6's proposed Math.fround enables fragile optimizations. (2) SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data)—a specification proposal (by John McCutchen, Google) for float32x4 and vector types could deliver 300% speedups for parallel operations; collaboration involves Google, Mozilla, Intel, and TC39. (3) Threads—Web Workers exist but prohibit shared memory to prevent data races; enabling multi-threaded access requires careful standardization.

Demonstrations include the JavaScript MESS project (emulating retro CPUs), a Bullet physics simulation with 500 cubes at 50–60 fps, and Banana Bread (Sauerbraten engine port) running alongside an embedded Doom game in a web worker—both at 60 fps on average hardware. The Doom integration required less than 100 lines of code, highlighting web platform benefits beyond performance.

talks.title: "Thinking DSLs for Massive Visualization" by Leo Meyerovich (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how program synthesis can generate regular expressions, SQL and parallel visualization code from examples and partial programs.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for program synthesis, where the tool searches for a program that matches input-output examples, instead of programmers hand-writing dense symbolic code. Leo Meyerovich starts with regular expressions built by demonstration on file listings, then adds a partial program as a hint to guide the search. He describes his first prototype, which simply enumerated candidate expressions, and a later version built on the Rosette framework, which encodes the search as SMT constraints solved by Z3.

He then applies the same idea to SQL, synthesizing a set-difference query that lists students who had not signed up for meetings, using positive and negative examples. Trends in supercomputer speed and SAT solver capacity are used to argue that search-based synthesis will scale to larger programs. The second half covers a browser-style visualization engine that filters and lays out about 100,000 data points in real time. Its layout language is compiled to parallel JavaScript and GPU code, with layout modeled as tree traversals. Traversal schedules can be given as synthesis input, so a change that introduces a dependency breaking parallelism is rejected.

The takeaway for practitioners is to keep the examples and schedules next to the code so maintainers can see the intent, and to build synthesis primitives into domain-specific languages so the compiler does the heavy search work.

talks.title: "Servo: Designing and Implementing a Parallel Browser" by Jack Moffitt (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores how Servo's experimental Rust browser engine runs script, layout and iframes in parallel.
talks.summary:
Jack Moffitt of Mozilla Research presents Servo, an experimental browser engine written from scratch in Rust. He argues that mainstream browsers carry path-dependent design choices from about fifteen years ago, such as script blocking the HTML parser and a serial loop between script and layout. The aim is to find which ideas work, and to build a browser that is safer and easier to change than multi-million-line codebases.

The core experiments are running script and layout concurrently, using a copy-on-write DOM where layout reads a stable snapshot while script edits a separate copy, and parallelising layout passes over a separate flow tree. Rust's type system restricts each traversal to children, which prevents data races at compile time. Iframes run in their own tasks, so cross-origin frames, and same-origin frames marked sandboxed, can work in parallel. In a live demo, an animation and the browser UI kept running during a long matrix multiplication inside an iframe, while the same test froze the UI in a Gecko-based browser. Servo also isolates crashes, so a failing iframe shows an error instead of taking down the page. Partial layout lets a script read an element's position early, with the answer sent by message while layout continues.

At the time of the talk Servo passed the Acid1 test, had GPU rendering and compositing, basic DOM APIs and a quadtree tile manager, and still lacked incremental layout and benchmarks. Moffitt says Rust itself is part of the experiment, and that the team will change Rust if its abstractions fall short. He closes by inviting contributors, pointing to easy issues on GitHub.

talks.title: "Gershwin: Stack-based, Concatenative Clojure" by Daniel Gregoire (2013)
talks.teaser: Presents Gershwin, a stack-based extension of Clojure, and how its words and quotations change how code is written.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at the Emerging Languages Camp, the speaker introduces Gershwin, an additive, experimental extension to Clojure that introduces a stack-based, concatenative programming model inspired by languages like Forth and Factor. The project was conceived to scratch two main exploration itches: investigating the concatenative paradigm and achieving a deeper understanding of Clojure's compiler internals. By building directly on top of Clojure, Gershwin enables developers to utilize point-free, data-flow-centric programming while retaining full access to Clojure’s hosted runtime, immutable collections, and concurrency constructs.

### Key Topics
- **Concatenative & Stack-Based Paradigm**: Programs operate on an implicit data stack without explicit invocation syntax, parentheses, or formal argument parameters. Execution flows from data directly into operations.
- **Vocabulary and Syntax of Gershwin**: Functions are referred to as 'words' defined using Forth-style colons (`:`). Anonymous functions are represented as 'quotations' with custom reader macro syntax. Parentheses are preserved exclusively to fall back to standard Clojure expressions.
- **Factoring and Mental Model**: Rather than traditional variable-based abstractions, concatenative programming relies on vigorous factoring—breaking out arbitrary sequences of data and operations into newly named words. When stack shuffling becomes noisy, higher-order data-flow combinators help manage the flow.
- **Data-Flow Combinators**: Borrowing directly from Factor, Gershwin avoids excessive low-level stack manipulation (such as `swap`, `dup`, `drop`, `nip`, `pick`, `over`) through combinators categorized into preserving (`dip`, `keep`), cleave (`cleave`, `tri`), spread (`spread`), and apply combinators.
- **Clojure as an Extension Base**: Comparing language structure to human linguistic mastery (phonetics, vocabulary, discourse), Clojure provides sound micro-level guarantees around identity, state, values, and time, making it an ideal bedrock for high-level language experiments.

### Technical Details
- **Compiler Modifications**: Gershwin compiles unmodified Clojure code and introduces additive changes to `LispReader`. It adds reader macros for quotations and Gershwin var resolution, extends the parser for `:` word definitions, and expands the pushback reader buffer to differentiate between keyword syntax and word definitions. At the compiler level, forms are translated into standard Clojure function invocations that either push values to the stack or execute words against it.
- **Stack Implementation**: The stack implements Clojure's `IPersistentStack` interface backed under the hood by Clojure vectors. It is stored as a dynamic var in `gershwin.core`, allowing isolated stacks per thread to prevent race conditions during parallel processing operations (like `pmap`).
- **Execution & Conditionals**: While many expressions read in reverse postfix compared to standard Clojure, conditionals such as `if` accept a boolean condition and two quotations (then/else branches) to delay evaluation until invoked.

### Takeaways
Concatenative programming acts essentially like Clojure’s thread-macro (`->`) built natively into the core syntax, excelling in data-transformation pipelines, shell scripting pipelines, and UI composition. Rather than replacing Clojure, Gershwin demonstrates how hosted Lisps can serve as flexible, reliable platforms for exploring alternative programming paradigms without sacrificing access to existing ecosystem libraries and runtime semantics.

talks.title: "Partitions for Everyone!" by Kyle Kingsbury (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how network partitions break popular distributed databases and which consistency guarantees actually hold when the network fails.
talks.summary:
Kyle Kingsbury opens by arguing that network partitions are unavoidable, because an asynchronous network can delay, drop, or reorder messages and a node cannot tell a slow peer from a dead one. He points to operational data from Microsoft and Google and to post-mortems from several companies, including a GitHub incident where a split brain exposed private repository information. To study these failures he presents Jepson, a harness that runs a cluster, injects partitions, and compares client-recorded results with the final database state.

Kingsbury applies this method to several systems. ZooKeeper fails cleanly: writes stop during the partition, and no acknowledged write is lost. NuoDB keeps acknowledged writes but blocks for long periods, sometimes well after the partition ends. Kafka's shrinking in-sync replica set can promote a stale leader, which loses acknowledged writes, so he recommends majority quorums. Riak and Cassandra rely on last-write-wins, which silently discards concurrent updates, and Cassandra's lightweight transactions lost data and deadlocked under his tests despite marketing claims.

His takeaways are to decide which liveness and safety guarantees a system really needs, to rely on logical clocks rather than wall time, and to avoid trusting vendor consistency claims. He recommends writing a test program that injects failures with tools such as iptables, skews clocks, and measures actual behaviour against the model you assumed.

talks.title: "Making Software Development Make Sense to Everyone" by Jen Myers (2013)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Making Software Development Make Sense to Everyone" by Jen Myers (2013).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In her keynote address, Jen Myers examines how the tech industry can make software development accessible and comprehensible to people from diverse backgrounds. Drawing on her experience as a designer, developer, and educator at Dev Bootcamp and Girl Develop It, Myers argues that broadening participation in technology requires treating culture and education as interfaces. Rather than attempting to rewrite an overwhelming cultural system all at once, technologists can create welcoming, supportive interfaces that lower barriers to entry, challenge harmful stereotypes, and elevate new learners.

### Key Topics
- **Demographic Disparities and Research**: Myers highlights findings from a September 2013 U.S. Census report indicating that women's participation in computing occupations has declined since 1990, young women's entry into STEM fields is slowing, and Black and Hispanic individuals remain severely underrepresented. She reviews psychological studies showing how subtle gendered language in job descriptions, stereotype threat, and societal expectations depress female test performance in math and physics, whereas self-affirmation or anonymous testing closes performance gaps.
- **The "Interface" Metaphor**: Comparing the complex culture of software development to a tangled, legacy codebase, Myers notes that developers do not need to overhaul an entire system overnight. Instead, creating targeted, user-centered entry points—such as accessible workshops—helps newcomers engage constructively with the system.
- **Personal Experience and "Unlocking the Clubhouse"**: Myers shares her background as a self-taught web designer from rural Ohio who felt isolated as the sole woman in her university computer science cohort. A pivotal conversation at a Carnegie Mellon youth camp and reading the study *Unlocking the Clubhouse* revealed that feelings of imposter syndrome and exclusion were widely shared by women across different skill levels, driven by systemic cultural factors rather than inherent lack of aptitude.
- **Grassroots Education Models**: Myers recounts founding the Columbus, Ohio chapter of Girl Develop It in 2011 and her work at Dev Bootcamp Chicago. She notes that women show immense interest in coding when provided with safe spaces that explicitly welcome questions and eliminate the fear of looking inexperienced.
- **Visibility, Role Models, and Inspiration**: Myers references historical examples—such as astronaut Sally Ride, science communicator Neil deGrasse Tyson, and actress Nichelle Nichols (whose role as Lieutenant Uhura on *Star Trek* prompted her to recruit women and minorities for NASA)—to demonstrate the necessity of visible role models. She contrasts these inspiring figures with prevailing anti-social developer stereotypes (such as the depiction of Mark Zuckerberg in *The Social Network*), arguing for public passion and "romance" in tech education over exclusionary elitism.

### Technical Details & Audience Q&A
- **Dev Bootcamp vs. Girl Develop It**: During the Q&A, Myers clarifies the operational differences between intensive nine-week immersive programs like Dev Bootcamp (which prepares beginners for software developer careers) and community-driven evening workshops like Girl Develop It. She reports increasing female representation in recent Dev Bootcamp cohorts and high retention and referral rates when educational environments prioritize psychological safety.
- **Actionable Allyship**: Addressing an audience member asking how men can effectively assist without oversimplifying complex problems, Myers recommends listening, providing practical mentorship (such as guiding beginners through their first open-source pull requests or reviewing conference talk abstracts), and supporting existing grassroots efforts where help is requested.

### Takeaways
The lack of diversity in software development does not stem from an absence of interest or ability, but from cultural barriers and psychological stereotypes. Addressing these challenges requires creating encouraging, accessible learning environments, cultivating visible and diverse role models, and actively mentoring newcomers rather than gatekeeping technical knowledge.

talks.title: "What Is a Strange Loop and What is it Like To Be One?" by Douglas Hofstadter (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores what a strange loop means, how perception simplifies the world, and why the self may be an illusion.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker reflecting on a conference named after a phrase he coined decades ago, then turns to what gives rise to the self and consciousness. He places living things and machines on a scale of respect, asking why a mosquito draws less concern than a dog, and adds thermostats, flush toilets and plants to the comparison. He argues that perception is a heavy act of reduction: a crowd of over a thousand people collapses into the single word "audience."

Simple creatures respond without concepts, much like a knee reflex, and concepts emerge gradually as nervous systems grow more complex. Human self-image is built from feedback from others, mirrors and experience. He recalls hitting what he calls a ceiling of abstraction during graduate mathematics, which forced him to leave the field. Using a story about France claiming it decided to invade Russia, he argues that people attribute causes to an imagined "I," while real causation happens at lower physical levels. A snack-buying stop at a gas station illustrates competing desires rather than free will.

He distinguishes the strange loop from video feedback, where a camera pointed at its own monitor creates nested images but involves no real perception or simplification. He concludes that the self is a useful abbreviation, closer to a rainbow or mirage than a solid object, and that the story we tell about ourselves is far less complete than the processes beneath it.

talks.title: "Privacy Governance & Explainability in ML/AI" by Jared Maslin
talks.teaser: Frames privacy as a full data lifecycle concern and surveys methods for finding and reducing privacy and bias risk in ML systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short history of data privacy, starting from GDPR and moving through US state laws, data residency rules and sector regulations such as HIPAA and PCI. The speaker argues that privacy covers the whole data lifecycle, from collection to deletion, and not only security. Trust, transparency and privacy by design are presented as ways to keep consumer data an asset rather than a liability, with privacy built into processes from the start instead of added after a breach or audit.

The middle section turns to machine learning, where explaining how a model reached a decision is hard and bias can enter through domain knowledge, the training data, or how outputs are later used. Risk in data is examined through k-anonymity, l-diversity and closeness, each presented with its known weaknesses. Model-level techniques include adversarial training, which penalises reliance on a sensitive attribute, a variational autoencoder approach that surfaces latent attributes the model leans on, and differential privacy, which adds controlled noise to query answers. For documentation, model cards and a multi-dimensional privacy analytic are described as ways to record intended use, metrics, and potential harms.

The closing argument is that these checks should run as a repeatable part of agile work, such as during story grooming or retrospectives. Developers, engineers and data scientists are presented as the people best placed to supply the design context that lawyers, privacy offices and auditors need to assess risk.

talks.title: "Apache Pulsar and the Legacy of Telegraphy" by Jowanza Joseph
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Apache Pulsar and the Legacy of Telegraphy" by Jowanza Joseph.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Jowanza Joseph, a software engineer at Pluralsight, draws parallels between historical telegraphy—often referred to as the "Victorian Internet"—and modern distributed publish/subscribe systems, specifically Apache Pulsar. Joseph examines how early telegraph networks (both wired switchboard systems and wireless Morse code networks) grappled with foundational distributed systems challenges, including message switching, interception, cipher-based encryption, multi-point transmission, and message loss. He then details how Apache Pulsar's decoupled, layered architecture addresses these legacy challenges at cloud scale with modern durability, encryption, and stream processing mechanisms.

### Key Topics
- **The Legacy of Telegraphy:** Early telegraph networks faced severe operational hurdles, including privacy risks from switchboard operators intercepting messages, weak manual ciphers easily cracked by authorities, delivery uncertainty, and difficulties handling multi-subscriber broadcasting.
- **Pulsar Architecture & Decoupled Storage:** Originally developed at Yahoo and governed by the Apache Software Foundation, Apache Pulsar separates compute brokers from storage nodes via Apache BookKeeper, with coordination managed by Apache ZooKeeper. This separation allows storage and broker compute to scale independently.
- **Schema Enforcement & Tiered Storage:** Pulsar manages data transmission and validation via a built-in schema registry supporting formats like Avro and JSON Schema to handle schema evolution. For cost-effective retention, it provides tiered storage offloading from BookKeeper into Amazon S3 and Glacier while maintaining a unified read API.
- **Delivery Guarantees & Multi-Casting:** Pulsar supports robust publish/subscribe multi-casting and gives users configurable delivery guarantees, ranging from low-latency "at-least-once" delivery to "exactly-once" processing semantics.
- **Stream Processing & Serverless Functions:** Real-time analytics are enabled via Pulsar SQL (embedding Presto across live and tiered data) and lightweight, serverless Pulsar Functions (written in Java, Python, or Go) running directly on nodes or isolated inside Docker containers.

### Technical Details
- **Components:** Pulsar consists of client-facing broker nodes, Apache BookKeeper for persistent append-only immutable log storage, and Apache ZooKeeper for distributed consensus and cluster state.
- **Security & Data Ingress:** Ingress data validation is performed against the schema registry using Avro schema evolution (e.g., modifying fields to accept null values). Message transmission over the wire is secured out of the box using SSL.
- **Tiered Storage Architecture:** BookKeeper acts as "hot" storage; as data ages, Pulsar can automatically offload segment data to cold tiers like AWS S3 and Glacier. Client consumers continue reading via the identical Pulsar API without modifying query logic.
- **Stream Processing Engine:** Pulsar SQL embeds Presto workers capable of executing distributed SQL queries spanning hot BookKeeper logs and archived S3/Glacier storage. Pulsar Functions support single-input-to-output topic event processing, with community interest in native sinks (e.g., Elasticsearch, Couchbase, CockroachDB).

### Takeaways
Modern pub/sub architectures like Apache Pulsar solve historical networking and message-routing vulnerabilities through independent scaling, strong schema governance, native SSL encryption, and flexible tiering. By isolating compute from storage, systems can seamlessly handle multi-petabyte datasets, maintain unified SQL query capabilities across hot and cold archives, and run serverless stream processing workloads efficiently.

talks.title: "Unison: a new distributed programming language" by Paul Chiusano
talks.teaser: Explains how Unison identifies code by content hash to drop builds, dependency conflicts, and repeated test runs.
talks.summary:
Paul Chiusano introduces Unison, an open-source, statically typed functional language built around identifying every definition by a hash of its content rather than by its name. Each definition is stored as a serialized syntax tree, with names kept as separate metadata. Because the syntax tree refers to dependencies by hash, a function can be renamed without breaking downstream users, and each dependency is pinned to an exact version.

The talk then follows the consequences of that choice. Since stored definitions never change, their types can be looked up instead of re-checked, and test results can be cached against their hashes. Chiusano argues that diamond dependency conflicts stop being a real problem when two versions of a library can coexist under different hashes, and that typed durable storage can work without hand-written JSON encoders and decoders. A live demo in the code base manager showed type-based search, watch expressions whose results are cached on save, tests that reuse cached outcomes after a rename, and a semantic history of changes.

The closing section covers distributed programming. A node can be sent a hash and asks only for the definitions it lacks, so nodes do not need preconfigured code. Distributed execution is expressed through an ability whose interpreters are ordinary library code, illustrated with a toy distributed merge sort. Chiusano notes that this batch-computing model is usable now, while stateful elastic services remain active research. A public alpha is being tested, with details on the project website.

talks.title: "The strange loop making parasitic insects our friends" by Mary Marek-Spartz
talks.teaser: Shows how host-parasitoid population models built on recursive equations can guide biological control of invasive garlic mustard.
talks.summary:
Biological control fights invasive plants and pests by releasing natural enemies from their native range. The speaker, an entomology PhD student, explains that many of the most useful control agents are parasitoids, insects that develop inside or on a host and kill it. Ecologists have modeled these host-parasitoid pairs since the early 1900s with Nicholson-Bailey recurrence equations, which are naturally recursive. The talk traces how a 2005 model of an annual weed, Patterson's curse, was fitted to field data to reproduce the stable coexistence seen in the field.

The speaker applies the same approach to garlic mustard, a forest invader that is a strict biennial with a seed bank lasting up to seven years. The model separates the seed bank, the rosette stage and the flowering adult stage, and links them with recursive functions for two weevils: one that attacks rosettes and one that attacks flowering stems. The model is packaged as a Python library called generations, with a configuration file of parameters, memoized functions to avoid recalculating past steps, and a graphing step that turns output into an interactive chart.

The speaker stresses that the model is simplified, since germination, decay and weevil attack rates vary widely in the field and need better data. The goal is to compare which agent combinations give enough control, not to predict field outcomes. Before release, agents are tested for host range in containment; for garlic mustard, 114 native plants were tested and the weevils developed only on the target. Planned work includes sensitivity analysis, hyperparasitism and environmental variables.

talks.title: "Automating Operations of a Global CDN" by Robert Fernandes
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix's Open Connect CDN is run and how its tools team automates operations.
talks.summary:
Robert Fernandes opens with a primer on content delivery networks, which place servers geographically close to users so that content travels shorter paths. He explains how this reduces metered transit costs and congestion for internet providers, and notes that Netflix streaming reportedly accounted for about a third of US internet traffic at peak hours. He then describes why Netflix built its own Open Connect network instead of relying on third-party CDN providers, which meant taking on the full end-to-end process of deploying and maintaining servers.

The talk walks through the Open Connect hardware: storage appliances that hold most of the catalogue on spinning disks, and flash appliances built for higher throughput. Netflix deploys thousands of sites with over 10,000 appliances, either inside partner ISP facilities or at Netflix-managed exchange points. Content is pre-loaded during off-peak hours, and a tiered fill process lets a few machines fetch from upstream while others copy from their local neighbours. Fernandes then covers the tools team's charter, which is to make operations more efficient and reliable across inventory, legal and accounting records, monitoring, and partner portals. He describes how early processes relied on spreadsheets, scripts and email, and lists warning signs in legacy three-tier applications, such as features forcing whole-application scaling. The team is moving toward domain services, a gateway layer, and GraphQL for user interfaces.

The main takeaway is pragmatic: MVC frameworks remain a sound choice for small projects, and decomposing a system makes sense once operational burden grows. Teams running physical fleets should expect manual processes to persist alongside automation, and aim to shrink them rather than eliminate them entirely.

talks.title: "Myths and Metaphors of Open Source" by Daniel Compton
talks.teaser: Examines how metaphors shape the way open-source work is funded, valued and designed, and proposes partnership as a better frame.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the metaphors people use for open source shape how they value the maintainers who build it. Daniel Compton starts with older metaphors for the brain, from Roman plumbing to telephone exchanges to computers, to show how an imperfect analogy can mislead. He then turns to computing's own metaphors, such as the desktop from the Xerox Star and the teletype behind the command line, and to the "real UNIX hacker" myth from the jargon file.

Next he examines framings applied to open source: competition, the commons, infrastructure, donations, patronage and the vending machine. Each captures something useful but breaks down in places. The commons idea fails because software can be copied without being used up, and patronage can bring sponsor influence over a project. Interface design matters too. GitHub's issue tracker asks little of reporters, and its contribution streaks pushed maintainers into unsustainable daily work until GitHub removed them. Compton also describes Clojure funding group Clojure's Together, where a $150 hourly rate drew complaints, while a flat $1,800 monthly payment for the same money was better received.

He proposes partnership as the frame: an exchange in which users give time, money or attention, and projects return valuable software. Support should be freely given, not forced. He closes by asking listeners to treat dependencies as work done by people, support the projects they rely on, and consider what behaviour their own platforms encourage.

talks.title: "RGB to XYZ: The Science and History of Color" by John Austin
talks.teaser: Traces how the 1931 CIE color standards shaped RGB and modern displays, and why color math often goes wrong.
talks.summary:
The talk opens in 1931, during the Great Depression, when delegates met in France at the CIE conference to agree on a shared color standard. Precise color naming mattered for signal lights on ships and planes as trade grew. The US representative, Irwin Priest, arrived angry about the short notice he had received for the proposals and clashed with the British scientist John Guild, whose additive-primary system was up for a vote. The two spent a week debating before the conference adopted a revised framework.

The speaker then explains how human color vision works: three types of cones respond to different parts of the spectrum, which is why different light spectra can look identical (metamers) and why displays can fake colors. Guild's experiments produced CIE RGB, which needed negative values, and that led to CIE XYZ, an all-positive, linear space in which the Y value tracks brightness. In the 1970s sRGB was designed for digital displays and adds a nonlinear gamma curve, so arithmetic done directly on sRGB values gives wrong results. The talk notes that game engines moved to linear sRGB for lighting after 2010, which improved their rendering.

The talk closes with CIE Lab, which is designed to be perceptually uniform, so gradients and grayscale conversions look more natural. A sunflower example showed a grayscale conversion done in RGB looking darker and producing odd white spots, while Lab kept brightness consistent. The practical takeaway is to choose a color space that fits the task, avoid doing math in sRGB, and remember that CMYK print values depend on the specific printer, ink and paper.

talks.title: "Probabilistic scripts for automating common-sense tasks" by Alexander Lew
talks.teaser: Shows how probabilistic programming can replace brittle heuristic cleaning scripts with declarative domain knowledge and Bayesian inference.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces probabilistic scripting, a declarative style of programming that takes ideas from probabilistic programming languages and applies them to everyday software problems. The running example is cleaning a small apartment listings table with misspelled cities, missing states and implausible rents. A simple script that snaps each city to the nearest match and fills in the state from it produces Beverly Hills in Missouri, Newark in New York and Seattle in Alabama, showing how tie-breaking heuristics pile up and still fail.

The speaker argues that Bayes' rule gives a principled alternative. Domain knowledge, such as larger cities appearing more often, rents being similar within a city, and typos being rare, forms a prior, and each observed row is scored against candidate values by how well they explain it. Logic programming is dismissed because the needed constraints are not known in advance, and neural networks are judged poor fits because they need labeled training data and are hard to maintain.

The prototype, P-Clean, is a small language embedded in Julia where users write random generators for each column. These compile into a model in the Gen probabilistic programming language, and approximate inference performs the cleaning. Unknown parameters can be left blank and learned from the messy table with expectation maximization. A second example uses GPT-2 inside a model of Amazon reviews conditioned on sentiment and product type. The takeaway is to frame a problem as inference over unknowns given domain knowledge and observations, and the speaker reports preliminary results that match existing machine-learning cleaning systems when basic domain knowledge is encoded.

talks.title: "Learning to Love JavaScript" by Tara Vancil
talks.teaser: Argues that JavaScript's flaws helped it spread and that the open web is a shared human achievement worth protecting.
talks.summary:
This talk, delivered as a historical and cultural argument rather than a practical coding guide, presents the web as a shared standard that many organizations and individuals have agreed to follow. The speaker describes the values built into it: anyone can take part, no single company or government owns it, and keeping it working is a collective responsibility. Drawing on personal experience, including building an experimental peer-to-peer browser with a two-person team and later working on an in-browser editing platform, the speaker explains a long-standing interest in lowering the barriers to publishing on the web.

The central claim is that JavaScript should be judged in its social and political context, not solely as a programming language. The speaker acknowledges that it was written quickly and has well-known weaknesses, but argues those weaknesses are part of why it became so widely used, and that removing it would break decades of existing pages. The talk cites Tim Berners-Lee's principle of least power and a blog post by Jeff Atwood on the reach of JavaScript. It then showcases playful and useful web projects as evidence of what the platform makes possible, and credits Let's Encrypt with making free TLS certificates widely available.

The talk closes by asking listeners to keep criticism of JavaScript constructive and to consider contributing to standards work in TC39 if they have concerns about the language. Along the way it includes a brief aside on collective action among tech workers. The main takeaway is an appreciation for the web's cooperative history and a reminder that its maintenance depends on the people who build on it.

talks.title: "Community Driven Development" by Christine Zagrobelny
talks.teaser: Shows how a developer built and sustained software for an immigrant rights nonprofit through volunteer community building.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the New Sanctuary Coalition, a New York group led by immigrants that resists detention and deportation. Its programs include accompanying people to immigration check-ins, a weekly pro se legal clinic, an anti-detention effort with a bond fund, and physical sanctuary in religious spaces. After the 2016 election, attendance at the clinic grew so fast that passing asylum application work between volunteers by hand became unsustainable. The speaker, a volunteer developer, built a Rails application as a minimum viable product, scoping it to a three-month timeline and to work the organization was already doing.

The speaker explains what maintaining the software required: bug fixes, feature requests, project management, security and uptime, plus training. In-person training worked better than video demos, which went out of date. Growth numbers are shared, with weekly accompaniments rising from about ten to between 50 and 70 friends, and clinic attendance restructured to stay near 100. Tech volunteers also handled unglamorous tasks such as email migration, laptop imaging and password manager setup, which the speaker argues matter as much as flashier programming work.

To attract long-term contributors, the speaker ran hack events, then wrote detailed issues with background sections describing the real-world need behind each one. Other steps included inviting contributors to see the work in person, a monthly newsletter, and virtual co-working nights. The closing advice is to find local organizations led by people directly affected by the issues, join their community first, and invest in that community so the technical work stays sustainable.

talks.title: "Computer Vision and NLP for Multi-Task Fashion Modeling" by Michael Sugimura
talks.teaser: Shows how a retailer combines image and text models in one multi-task network to tag fashion attributes at catalog scale.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes the problem at a Chicago-based e-commerce company that aggregates product catalogs from about 140 online retailers. Each retailer describes attributes such as color, pattern, sleeve length and cut in its own wording, so the team needs models that normalize millions of products without manual mappings. The same attribute features also feed visual similarity search.

The modeling approach uses hard parameter sharing in multi-task learning, where a shared backbone feeds separate classifier heads and the per-task losses are summed for backpropagation. The image branch passes both a full product photo and a center crop through a ResNet-50 and concatenates the features, which recovered detail lost when images were downscaled. The text branch fine-tunes BERT on titles, descriptions and brand fields. An ensemble joins the image and text feature vectors in a dense network, and the speaker reports it usually beats either model alone by several percentage points.

For adding new attributes, the team saves weights per network section, marks new heads as untrained, and reloads earlier weights into a changed layout. They also built a multi-dataset training pipeline in which each attribute has its own labeled dataset, batches are shuffled together, and loss is computed only for the labels present in each batch. The results matched a unified dataset and held up outside fashion. The speaker notes that subjective labels and keeping earlier weights frozen remain hard.

talks.title: "Compacting the Uncompactable" by Bobby Powers
talks.teaser: Explains how the Mesh allocator compacts C and C++ heaps by remapping pages, without relocating or updating pointers.
talks.summary:
Bobby Powers starts with memory fragmentation, where a long-running C or C++ program holds far more memory from the operating system than its live objects need. Garbage-collected runtimes can fix this by moving objects and rewriting pointers, but C and C++ binaries often hide pointers in tagged bits, stripped symbols, and registers, so that approach is unsafe.

The talk presents Mesh, a drop-in malloc replacement that needs no code changes or recompilation. It pairs partly full pages of the same size class whose live objects sit at non-overlapping offsets, copies one page's objects into the other at the same offsets, then remaps the virtual page onto the shared physical page so no addresses change. Randomized allocation keeps such pairs common; without it, the speaker said almost no memory was recovered. Pair selection is cast as matching, approximated in linear time by SplitMesher, rather than the NP-complete clique cover.

On Firefox running the Speedometer benchmark, average heap size fell about 17% while the score stayed within 1% of the default allocator. On a Redis LRU workload, Mesh recovered memory comparable to Redis's hand-written defragmentation routine using about five times fewer cycles. The speaker also noted Linux page-table limits and a segfault handler that holds writes to in-flight pages, and suggested bulk page-table updates as a possible speedup. The takeaway is that interpreters for languages like Ruby and JavaScript can gain compaction without touching their garbage collectors.

talks.title: "How We Tell Stories In Code" by Hannah Howard
talks.teaser: Argues that code is a way for people to communicate and shows what programmers can borrow from storytelling.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that code is mainly a way for people to communicate with each other, since computers run whatever they are given while humans must read, debug and maintain it. Tracing storytelling from cave drawings to film, the talk proposes that programmers should spend as much effort learning to tell good stories as they do learning languages and tools. It is aimed at people who have just entered the industry and are unsure how to keep improving.

The speaker recalls struggling as a young programmer, failing to build a 3D game engine and later finding the Doom source code plainer than expected. Patterns and frameworks are presented as helpful formulas that work for familiar problems but leave people on their own with new ones. Work as a grant writer for a small nonprofit showed the speaker how to pick a few key accomplishments and drop inconsistencies so an outsider could follow the story. Software gets the same treatment: every solution is partial, and the real problem space is usually larger than the team realises.

The practical takeaway is that code gets better through practice, feedback and revision rather than a fixed list of steps. Testing, pair programming and refactoring build revision into daily work, and stepping away from the screen is tied to creative breakthroughs. The speaker closes by advising people to hold their approaches loosely, let go of ideas that stop working, and treat each day's work as a draft. In the Q&A, journaling and reflection were suggested for becoming a better storyteller.

talks.title: "Complexities of Color in Computing" by Ellen Wondra
talks.teaser: Explores how human and machine color perception differ, and how color shapes accessibility, facial recognition and counter-surveillance.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how color works, starting with white light that objects partly absorb before it reaches the eye. It contrasts this subtractive model with screens, which build color additively from red, green and blue values. It explains why a simple Euclidean distance between RGB values does not match how people perceive differences in color, which led to perceptual measures such as Delta E and to gamma correction in photography.

The second part turns to accessibility. It covers the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines and why color should never be the only signal for an error or status, along with minimum contrast ratios for text and interface elements. It recounts how a 1950s Kodak print calibration card, based on a single pale-skinned model, left darker skin tones underserved for about twenty years. Modern facial recognition systems show similar gaps in accuracy across skin tone and gender, which the speaker links to unrepresentative test datasets.

The final section surveys counter-surveillance wearables that use color and infrared light to disrupt face detection. Examples include CV Dazzle makeup, patterned scarves, glasses that remap facial features, and infrared lights mounted on caps. The talk closes with the viral blue-and-black dress, which shows that the science of color perception is still incompletely understood. The takeaway for practitioners is to test software against diverse perception and data, and to avoid relying on color alone when conveying information.

talks.title: "Beyond Alt-Text: Trends in Online Accessibility" by Ian Forrest
talks.teaser: Walks developers through practical web accessibility fixes for keyboards, focus, alt text, headings, contrast, and workplace culture.
talks.summary:
Ian Forrest, an engineering manager at BiblioCommons, opens with accessibility terminology and the reasons it matters. He explains that disability is contextual and can change over time, describes assistive technologies such as screen readers, magnification and speech input, and uses the curb cut effect to show how features built for disabled users help everyone.

The core of the talk is a set of practical web checks. Keyboard navigation comes first, with examples of confusing tab order, removed focus outlines and skip links. Focus management in overlays is shown with a modal that traps keyboard users. Alt text guidance covers decorative images, collapsing duplicate links, avoiding positive tabindex values and adding screen-reader-only text to repeated link labels. Heading hierarchy, zoom behaviour with relative units, colour contrast ratios, high contrast themes and readability tools round out the checklist, each illustrated with live examples from library and retail sites.

The closing section covers workplace practice. Designers, product managers and developers all need training. Automated checkers such as pa11y catch simple problems, but complex issues like focus in overlays need testing with people who use assistive technology daily. Local meetups, internal documentation and a shared chat channel for feedback round out the advice. The takeaway is that accessible patterns benefit everyone and matter most to those who rely on them.

talks.title: "Assistive Augmentation: Lip Reading with AI" by Serg Masis
talks.teaser: Shows how a deep learning model that fuses lip video and audio tries to make speech readable for deaf users.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that hearing loss is largely invisible, affecting about ten million people at moderate to profound levels. Misconceptions persist, such as the belief that all deaf people sign or that lip reading is easy, and even professionals catch only a small share of speech from lips alone. Speech recognition struggles in noisy rooms, so the speaker proposed an ideal tool: a phone or tablet pointed at a speaker that displays the text beneath it.

To prototype this, the speaker fused video and audio in a deep learning model. Mouth regions were located with a facial landmark model and cropped to a fixed size, while the audio was converted to MFCC features. A watch branch of convolutional and LSTM layers read the lip frames, a listen branch handled sound, and a spell module with attention weighed which features to keep. Training used roughly 500 hours of TED talks, with about 100 hours held out for testing. The speaker compared the approach with earlier research from Google DeepMind on BBC footage, which reported nearly four times the roughly 12 percent professional lip-reading rate.

Demonstrations were mixed. Clear, slow speech worked well, but accents, fast delivery and rare words caused errors, such as an unusual word rendered as a common one. Punctuation like question marks was usually missed, because those cues depend on longer context than the training windows allowed. The speaker concluded that the dataset was too small for a full language and that a larger annotated corpus, a more complex model and faster inference would be needed before phone use. Combining sight and sound adds robustness, but practical use depends on data and efficiency.

talks.title: "Declarative APIs in an Imperative World" by Tilde Thurium
talks.teaser: Explains how to bridge declarative React components with imperative editor APIs, using Atom's git and focus code as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts declarative and imperative programming, using turn-by-turn driving directions versus simply entering an address to show the difference. It argues that declarative UI frameworks such as React help avoid a class of state-management bugs, comparing a list add-and-remove widget written in plain DOM code with its React version. The speaker notes that abstractions leak and that declarative styles often bring their own domain-specific syntax.

The main case study covers integrating React with imperative APIs from the Atom editor, including text editor state, panels rendered through portals, git integration, and focus management. Rather than rewriting Atom's APIs, which would have forced package authors to upgrade, the team wrapped each imperative API in a component that marks the boundary. Focus handling used refs, and "ref holders" deferred operations until a DOM node existed; the speaker links this pattern to the maybe monad. Global command registries forced props to be passed deep through the tree, a pain point the team had not fully solved.

The closing section asks why declarative UI took years to spread, arguing that web apps became far more complex and that programming trends react to earlier ones. It then turns to ageism in tech, suggesting objective interview rubrics, auditing job postings, and valuing code maintenance over constant rewrites. The takeaway is that no single integration pattern fits every case, and the right boundary depends on the imperative API being wrapped.

talks.title: "Voice Driven Development: Who needs a keyboard anyway?" by Emily Shea
talks.teaser: Shows how a software engineer with repetitive strain injury writes and ships code by voice using Talon and a custom alphabet.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the speaker's repetitive strain injury, which made typing painful and cut into working hours. Breaks, stretching, wrist braces, massage, physical therapy, an ergonomic assessment and a split keyboard all helped only partly, so the presenter turned to speaking code instead of typing it.

The setup combines a good microphone, Dragon dictation for speech recognition, and Talon, a free hands-free layer configured with Python scripts. Rather than the NATO alphabet, the speaker uses a custom set of short, one-syllable words that are less likely to be confused, and uses ordinal numbers to repeat commands. Live demos covered spelling, numbers, symbols, phrases, formatters and custom vocabulary, followed by a recorded session of editing and pushing Perl code in an editor. The talk also covered vocal strain, noisy open offices, and remote work as practical concerns.

The speaker advised setting aside dedicated time to learn, copying familiar code, pairing with a helper, and avoiding deadlines while learning. The main takeaway is that software should be accessible without a keyboard or mouse, since anyone may need those alternatives someday, and that voice and other non-touch input may become more common.

talks.title: "Deterministic Docker Images with Go Microservices" by Jon San Miguel
talks.teaser: Explains how to make Go service builds and Docker images byte-for-byte reproducible, cutting deploy times and unneeded redeployments.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why a team shipping many Go microservices would want reproducible builds. When the same code yields the same Docker digest, layers do not have to cross the network on every deploy, unchanged services can skip redeployment, and singleton services see less downtime during restarts. The speaker frames determinism as three steps: making Go compilation reproducible, making Docker builds reproducible, and reducing large dependency graphs.

On the Go side, binaries can embed package paths, linked object paths, and a random build ID. Compiling inside identical containers and using the internal linker removes most of this, except for a few services that cannot use it. For Docker, run steps and file timestamps prevent cache reuse when pipeline runs overlap, so the team used Bazel with distroless base images, which produce identical digests from identical input. Reflection also blocks dead-code removal, so unrelated changes in a package can still alter a binary.

To tame dependency chains, the speaker introduced two internal tools: depstat, which maps import graphs and attributes deploys to commits, and import checker, which enforces allowlisted import rules. Recommended practices include splitting large helper packages, separating frequently changed configuration from stable code, and pinning vendored dependencies. Build times fell from about an hour and a half, and hundreds of services could be deployed several times an hour.

talks.title: "Improving law interpretability using NLP" by Serena Peruzzo
talks.teaser: Shows how spaCy parsing and clustering can extract obligations and responsible entities from Ontario accessibility legislation.
talks.summary:
Serena Peruzzo presents a proof of concept built with a government of Ontario research group to make legislation easier to interpret. Legal text is hard to work with: it has no labeled training data, unusual bullet and reference formatting, long nested sentences, and domain-specific vocabulary.

The case study uses the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act and its regulation. The pipeline uses spaCy for tokenization, lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing. Sentences containing a short list of obligation verbs, expanded through WordNet synonyms into a lightweight ontology, were labeled as burdens; manual labeling of the text gave 89% accuracy and caught 97% of burdens. For each burden, a breadth-first walk of the dependency tree recovers the full subject phrase. Subjects were then normalized, averaged GloVe vectors, reduced with spectral embedding, and clustered with k-means, with the elbow method suggesting three clusters.

Clustering revealed three groups: transportation standards, physical barriers such as ramps, surfaces and stairs in public spaces, and administration with standards definitions. Public and private responsibilities were not clearly separated, and some duties remained ambiguous. The speaker presented the result as a reusable framework for explaining rules to citizens and organizations and for spotting unclear or duplicated provisions for lawmakers.
