talks.title: "Alda's dynamic relationship with Clojure" by Dave Yarwood
talks.teaser: Traces how a text-based music composition language evolved its architecture, from a Clojure server to a Go and Kotlin client.
talks.summary:
Dave Yarwood introduces Alda, a text format for writing music that a command-line client interprets and plays back, with editor integration for quick feedback. He contrasts this with visual, mouse-driven notation software, arguing that slow notation can push composers toward repetitive material. He also shows that Alda embeds Clojure expressions, so scores can use functions and sequences inside the markup.

The talk then traces the architecture through several phases. The first prototype was a single Clojure program, which suffered from slow startup and blocking playback. A second phase moved to a background server reached over HTTP, and a third swapped HTTP for ZeroMQ with a broker that routed requests to worker processes, which fixed audio glitches when several synthesizers ran at once. Phase five removed the server: a Go client starts a player process and drives it with OSC messages over UDP, and the code moved from Clojure to Go and Kotlin so it could ship as native executables. A separate Clojure library, alda-clj, generates Alda text for live coding. Demos included random melodic generators and a piece that maps National Weather Service forecasts to notes, with temperature setting pitch, wind direction setting stereo panning, and wind speed affecting tempo and volume.

The main lesson is that the design moved toward simplicity, with the client doing most of the work. Keeping Clojure as an inline scripting layer and a live-coding library preserved the creative workflow. Export to MIDI gives a rough starting point for sheet music, though it cannot always infer intended bar lines or enharmonic spellings.

talks.title: "Dive into Streams with Brooklin" by Celia Kung
talks.teaser: Explains how LinkedIn's Brooklyn streaming service moves data from many sources to many destinations at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Brooklyn, a streaming data pipeline service LinkedIn built to replace a patchwork of specialized change data capture systems. As LinkedIn's data spread across Oracle, Espresso, Kafka, and cloud services in Azure and AWS, nearline applications needed continuous, low-latency access without each team building its own pipelines. The speaker explains that Brooklyn aims to be multi-tenant, dynamically provisioned, and easy to extend with new sources and destinations.

Two main scenarios are covered: change data capture, where applications consume a change stream instead of querying a live database, and streaming bridges that move data between clouds or data centers. The speaker walks through a profile-update example and the architecture, in which a REST management service writes stream definitions to ZooKeeper, a leader distributes work as tasks, and consumers and producers pass events on to Kafka. A central case is the replacement of Kafka MirrorMaker, which had required hundreds of clusters. Brooklyn handles that work as pipelines in one cluster, with pause and auto-resume at the pipeline, topic, or partition level so that a single failing partition does not stall the rest.

The closing section covers production scale, with figures for daily message volume and stream counts, along with planned work on new sources, batching for storage destinations, auto-scaling, and pass-through compression, which the speaker says could raise mirroring throughput at least fivefold. Questions covered the Java-only implementation, comparisons with Kafka Connect and Debezium, how encryption policies are enforced through key management, and the project's open-source status. The main takeaway is that a centralized, extensible pipeline service can reduce operational burden compared with many one-off pipelines.

talks.title: "Beyond traces: the insights in trace aggregates" by Daniela Miao
talks.teaser: Shows how aggregating many distributed traces surfaces the customer, server, and lock behind production slowdowns.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a single distributed trace is rarely enough to diagnose a production problem, because it captures one request out of possibly millions. The speaker frames observability as needing analysis on top of raw telemetry, and proposes letting a machine compare hundreds or thousands of traces to surface what stands out.

The first case is an internal incident in which a customer unintentionally overloaded the ingestion system. Metric dashboards were hard to read, and the customer ID was too high-cardinality to be a default dashboard dimension, so finding it took hours. Comparing the slowest one percent of traces against the rest with a correlation score pointed to that customer's project within minutes. A second case involved long-tail latency at an early customer, where the slowest requests correlated almost perfectly with one server, which turned out to have a faulty network card. A more exploratory section looked at critical paths grouped by lock ID in a demo donut-ordering app. Chocolate orders held the topper lock far longer than other flavors, while cinnamon orders waited behind them.

The takeaway is that correlations are strong hints rather than proof, but they cut investigation time sharply. Practitioners should attach high-cardinality attributes to their traces and analyze groups of traces rather than individual ones. The speaker also recommends OpenTelemetry as an open standard for generating the telemetry needed to build those aggregates.

talks.title: "Finding bugs without running or even looking at code" by Jay Parlar
talks.teaser: Shows how describing a system in the Alloy model checker can expose design flaws before anyone reads or runs its code.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that design-level bugs can be found without running or reading code. The starting point is that explaining a system in writing, or to a knowledgeable listener, often exposes gaps in thinking. The main tool is Alloy, an MIT model checker, which takes a formal description of a system, searches the possible states it can reach, and reports any state that breaks a stated property. A small permission model with accounts, users and resources, where access to a parent resource extends to its children, is built up step by step. Each run surfaces a flaw in the spec: a user belonging to two accounts, a resource with no account, a resource listed as its own parent, and a case where inherited access fails to reach deeper children.

The middle of the talk covers real uses. In one project, a model of several customer portals, browser sessions and SAML logins produced a 13-step sequence that left the identity provider holding a token it could no longer revoke, and the developers had to delay a release to fix it. In another, a model built alongside an API's developer showed that the customer experience team misunderstood what the API could do, so a year of work was discarded before six teams built on it. Pamela Zave's Alloy analysis of the Chord protocol found counterexamples to all seven correctness claims in the original paper.

The closing takeaways are to write designs down in something other than code, to model existing systems to learn how they behave, and to model new systems early, when changes are still cheap. The speaker points to the Alloy book, an online architecture chapter, and TLA+ resources for anyone who wants to start.

talks.title: "Scala DSLs and Probabilistic Programming" by Joe Wingbermuehle
talks.teaser: Shows how Stan probabilistic models can be embedded in Scala, with compile-time type checks and scope rules for model code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a simple task: predicting weight from height. The speaker writes a linear model with normal error as a generative model, then hands inference to Stan, a probabilistic programming language that samples from the posterior instead of returning a single point estimate. Adding separate intercepts and slopes for each gender shows how a model can be extended with little code, and the result is still imperfect, which motivates further modelling.

The core argument is for embedding Stan inside Scala rather than loading Stan files or concatenating strings. The benefits covered are editor autocompletion of distributions, type errors reported at the line where they occur, composable model pieces that can be combined into larger models, and room for linting, such as warning when a standard deviation has no lower bound. The implementation represents Stan types as Scala types, uses implicit type classes to reject invalid operations such as dividing a scalar by a vector, restricts random number draws to the blocks where Stan allows them, and checks input data against declarations at compile time.

Break and continue statements are harder to validate by types alone, so the speaker adds a pass over the abstract syntax tree that tracks loop nesting with a state monad and rejects a break outside a loop before any Stan code is generated. The library is open source, and most Stan functions are supported, though newer functions take effort to keep up with. The takeaway is that encoding a domain's rules in the host language's type system catches model errors early and makes reusable models easier to build on.

talks.title: "Designing Augmented Reality Systems for Speed" by Diana Hu
talks.teaser: Explores how augmented reality apps meet real-time limits through systems design, low-latency networking, and actor-model concurrency.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "Designing Augmented Reality Systems for Speed," Diana Hu, head of the AR engineering team at Niantic Labs (makers of Pokémon GO and acquirers of Escher Reality), examines the technical challenges of making augmented reality fast, reliable, and pervasive on commodity mobile hardware. While science fiction has long envisioned ubiquitous AR, practical AR systems must simultaneously solve interdisciplinary problems across computer vision, robotics, computer graphics, and distributed systems within tight thermal, battery, and latency budgets.

### Key Topics
- **Fundamental Hurdles of AR**: Hu outlines why AR remains difficult. Computer vision requires both semantic understanding (recognizing objects via deep learning models that typically require power-hungry GPUs) and geometric perception (understanding 3D space, depth, and spatial navigation, derived from robotics). Graphics rendering must realistically integrate digital objects with complex real-world lighting variations. Additionally, developer toolchains (e.g., Unity, Unreal) still face lengthy 5- to 15-minute iteration cycles because the real world lacks fixed boundaries.
- **Trends in Hardware and Telecommunications**: Projecting the future of AR, Hu highlights Koomey's law (battery requirements falling by half every 1.5 years for fixed compute loads), demonstrating that an iPhone 7 benchmarks comparably to older MacBook models. Referencing Richard Feynman's 1985 calculations on physical limits of computation and Holmes's law of telecommunications, she notes that cellular speeds inevitably converge toward Wi-Fi and wireline bandwidths (e.g., 5G targeting 10 Gbps), eventually matching human visual processing capacities.
- **Treating Mobile Devices Like Distributed Servers**: As multi-core mobile processors become standard, AR architectures should adopt proven distributed system design patterns, such as colocation, caching, remoting, sharding, and concurrency without blocking locks.

### Technical Details
- **Speeding Up Networking**: AR requires rendering at ~30 frames per second, necessitating response latencies within a 33 ms frame budget. Traditional client-server architectures route camera pose data from a phone through a cell tower to a remote cloud data center (e.g., in Virginia or Iceland) and back, incurring hundreds of milliseconds of latency. Niantic addressed this by eliminating cloud hops for localization updates. By establishing a direct, peer-to-peer mesh connection through local cell towers between co-located devices, multiplayer tracking achieved latency in the tens of milliseconds. A hybrid protocol approach combines UDP for low-latency peer-to-peer pose broadcasting with TCP/server connections for anti-cheat authority and larger asset transfers.
- **Speeding Up Computation via the Actor Model**: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) pipelines ingest high-bandwidth sensor feeds (an uncompressed 1080x720 video feed at 30 fps requires ~600 Mbps of processing) and split work across feature tracking, localization, and mapping blocks. Naive implementations rely heavily on mutexes, shared state, and busy-waiting loops, causing computation cycles to exceed 1 second on embedded architectures. Niantic decoupled the SLAM pipeline using an actor model: camera inputs, feature extraction, localization, and mapping run as isolated actors communicating through message queues and internal sequential mailboxes. Without altering underlying computer vision math or algorithms, removing lock contention and busy-waiting yielded a 5x speedup.

### Takeaways
Rather than waiting for new mathematical breakthroughs or specialized hardware, significant performance gains in augmented reality can be realized immediately by applying mature distributed systems paradigms—such as peer-to-peer mesh networking and lock-free, message-passing actor architectures—directly to mobile AR software.

talks.title: "Algorithms for DNA Data Storage" by Ruthie Nachmany
talks.teaser: Traces how digital data came to be encoded in DNA, from early experiments to modern error-correcting and random-access methods.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growing gap between the data being produced and the capacity of current storage media. It cites limits on hard disk density, the degradation of magnetic tape, and the archival needs of large scientific and genomic projects. DNA is presented as a dense, durable medium, but the speaker also covers its drawbacks: high synthesis and sequencing costs, slow reads and writes, and strands that mutate or drop out.

The middle of the talk walks through the field's milestones in order. Early work in 2001 mapped letters to nucleotide combinations, and 2009 brought Huffman coding for compression. Later efforts added error correction, including a 2012 block-based scheme and a 2013 study that stored overlapping chunks, followed by Reed-Solomon codes in 2015. Random access, first proposed in 2015 and demonstrated at larger scale in 2018, allowed specific files to be retrieved without sequencing everything. The 2017 DNA Fountain method used fountain codes to approach the theoretical capacity of DNA. Other threads included error correction tailored to cheaper nanopore sequencers, CRISPR-based recording of edits in living bacteria, and image search over photos stored in DNA.

The closing section covers efforts to lower costs, such as prefabricated DNA fragments that are assembled rather than synthesized base by base. It also surveys emerging uses, including cold storage of cryptocurrency keys, DNA computing, and hybrid electronic-molecular devices. The main takeaway is that progress will depend on combining coding theory, information theory, molecular biology and engineering.

talks.title: "A Little Taste of Dependent Types" by David Christiansen
talks.teaser: Gives a gentle live tour of dependent types in the small language Pi, from natural numbers to proofs about evenness.
talks.summary:
The talk traces dependent type theory back to an early twentieth-century debate over what mathematics is. It contrasts Hilbert's view of mathematics as rule-governed symbol play with Brouwer's intuitionism, where mathematical objects live in mental constructions. Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, developed from the 1970s, and the calculus of constructions later shaped proof assistants and languages such as Agda and Idris. The speaker's book, The Little Typer, co-written with a colleague, uses a deliberately small language called Pi that does not automate away the difficult steps, so readers can see how the system works.

The live demo walks through Pi one step at a time. Numbers, atoms and pairs are checked against their types, and type errors appear when a value does not match its description. Two values that compute to the same result are recognised as the same, even inside a function. Because recursion is not allowed in Pi, addition and doubling are built from eliminators that expose a value's structure. Types then double as propositions: a pair is evidence for "and", a function is evidence for "implies", and a dependent pair captures "there exists". The speaker proves that zero is even and that every natural number is either even or odd, and the resulting program returns a number's parity along with its half.

The main takeaway is intuition rather than mastery. A single program can be both a computation and a machine-checked proof, and the talk points listeners to the book and to library copies for further study.

talks.title: "The Glitching Hour" by Amy Wibowo
talks.teaser: Explains how JPEG compression works and how corrupting its data on purpose produces glitch art effects.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Amy Wibowo (known online as sailor HG) explores digital aesthetics, focusing on how image compression mechanisms can be understood and manipulated to create artistic "glitch" effects. Paralleling how digital filters recreate analog camera imperfections like light leaks and film grain, she examines how digital compression artifacts and file corruption can produce nostalgic visual aesthetics.

### Key Topics
- **Digital Image Fundamentals and Bitmap Glitching**: A basic digital image consists of color samples (pixels) arranged in rows and columns, typically represented as red, green, and blue (RGB) values or hue, saturation, and value. Straightforward uncompressed formats like BMP precede sequential pixel data with headers (width, height, color space). In raw pixel data, glitches can be achieved directly by sorting pixel rows/columns, shifting spatial sections, or shifting individual color channels.
- **Lossless vs. Lossy Compression**: Compression reduces storage space while preserving discernible meaning. Lossless compression removes redundancies (such as counting consecutive identical characters) and allows exact reconstruction. Lossy compression discards details that are hard to notice (analogous to stripping vowels and punctuation from text).
- **JPEG Color Channel Separation**: JPEG reduces file size by dividing image details into varying layers. Splitting RGB into luminance, blue-green, and red-green channels takes advantage of human visual perception, which is much less sensitive to color shifts than brightness. Because luminance contains the primary detail, color channels can be stored at half resolution with minimal perceptible degradation.
- **Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) & Quantization**: Using an analogy of separating a string quartet recording into frequency tracks (violins, viola, cello) via Fourier analysis, the speaker explains how images behave like 2D waveforms. A Discrete Cosine Transform decomposes 8x8 pixel blocks into 64 2D basis functions. High-frequency coefficients (representing fine details) typically contribute less and are zeroed out or reduced by dividing by a quantization matrix determined by the JPEG quality setting.

### Technical Details
- **JPEG Artifacting**: Setting the JPEG quality setting very low discards high-frequency detail aggressively. Because each 8x8 block is transformed independently, block boundaries misalign and become visibly prominent, while sharp edges approximated by cosine sums exhibit halos or oscillations.
- **Targeted Byte Corruption**: Glitching compressed JPEGs without rendering the file unreadable requires avoiding image headers and metadata. Modifying only the compressed image stream—found after the `FF DA` section marker—ensures file decoders still parse the image.
- **Renderer Differences and Error Propagation**: Replacing a random byte in the compressed payload produces vastly different outcomes depending on how specific image decoders handle invalid data:
  - In Safari, corruption errors often terminate after a single row.
  - In Chrome, errors propagate across the rest of the image because the baseline (0,0) DC component of an 8x8 block is encoded differentially from previous blocks.
  - Byte corruption can alter location values, displacing blocks, or hit separate color channels to cause sweeping hue shifts.
  - Decoders like macOS preview render exposed basis function patterns differently.

### Takeaways
Understanding the mathematical foundations of JPEG compression—from color space subsampling and 8x8 DCT quantization to differential block encoding and file markers (`FF DA`)—allows creators to intentionally induce precise aesthetic glitches. Blending intentional quantization artifacting with targeted compressed-byte corruption enables complex artistic effects across web and desktop decoders.

talks.title: "Building a Canary Testing Framework" by Iheanyi Ekechukwu
talks.teaser: Walks through building a Go-based canary daemon that runs scripted tests against production systems on a schedule.
talks.summary:
Canaries are tests that run continuously against production to catch failures before users notice them. The speaker separates them from canary deployments and from ordinary integration tests, which often stop at the database layer. Drawing on networking work at DigitalOcean, the speaker describes canaries that create droplets, connect over SSH and verify traffic between them, and one canary that exposed a firewall race condition locking users out after a rule was applied right after creation.

The framework is built around a Go daemon that schedules each test on its own goroutine, runs it inside an embedded JavaScript virtual machine, and saves results to a key-value store. The stated requirements include concurrent and repeated runs, per-test timeouts, Prometheus metrics for running, passed and failed tests, and a GraphQL API for viewing results. The talk walks through loading configuration files, adding helper functions for reading secrets, making HTTP requests and emitting structured logs, then shows how the scheduler applies deadlines and records metrics.

A live demo runs a simple HTTP test and a deliberately failing one, with the results queried over GraphQL. The main takeaways are to give each product its own canary so results stay separate, and to use a loosely typed scripting language so checks are quick to write and change.

talks.title: "Leverage vs. Autonomy in a Large Software System" by Jake Donham
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Leverage vs. Autonomy in a Large Software System" by Jake Donham.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Jake Donham discusses how large engineering organizations balance leverage and autonomy when designing software architecture, drawing heavily on his experiences at Twitter. By applying organizational management principles—specifically Andy Grove’s concepts of functional versus mission-oriented teams and Conway's Law—Donham examines how software architecture affects developer productivity and efficiency. He traces Twitter’s evolution from an early Ruby monolith to a sprawling microservices ecosystem, and ultimately to Strato, a centralized platform designed to offer high operational leverage without stripping developer autonomy.

### Key Topics
- **Organizational Principles and Conway's Law**: Applying Andy Grove's team archetypes (functional teams offering leverage and economies of scale vs. mission-oriented teams optimizing for speed and autonomy) to system design. The talk references Conway’s Law (systems mirror communication structures) and Copeland's Law (mismatches between organization structure and software architecture cause operational friction).
- **Autonomy vs. Leverage Trade-offs**: Centralized systems maximize leverage and consistency but introduce single points of failure, monoculture risks, gatekeeping, and arcane knowledge. Decentralized architectures enhance local autonomy and decouple deployments, but lead to duplicated work, poor leverage, gratuitous variation, and severe difficulty in managing cross-cutting concerns.
- **Twitter’s Architectural Evolution**: The historical shift from a massive monolithic Ruby on Rails application (fraught with deploy queues, lack of modularity, and cross-cutting bugs) to an expansive microservices architecture (which improved autonomy but resulted in high per-service overhead, orphaned services, and fragmented cross-cutting libraries).
- **Architectural Sweet Spots**: Examples where centralization yielded massive leverage without sacrificing meaningful autonomy, notably Aurora/Mesos for cloud compute scheduling and Finagle for RPC communication, load balancing, failure detection, and service discovery.

### Technical Details
- **Compute and RPC Infrastructure**: Moving from manual host allocation and ad hoc deploy scripts to Aurora/Mesos provided automated scheduling, standardized configuration, and higher utilization on the JVM. Replacing raw Apache Thrift clients with Finagle delivered transparent RPC multiplexing, failure detection, distributed tracing, and futures-based asynchronous handling.
- **Microservices Challenges at Twitter**: Decomposing systems purely by domain nouns (e.g., users, tweets) led to awkward cross-cutting feature libraries embedded in client services, creating distributed deploy dependencies, ownership vacuums, and ad hoc internal platforms.
- **Strato Platform Architecture**: Strato addresses these issues by acting as a centrally operated monolithic platform hosting microservices defined as lightweight configurations. It isolates system concerns (timeouts, retries, RPC infrastructure) from business logic, and decouples platform code deployments from fast, frequent configuration deployments.
- **StratoQL DSL**: Strato services execute logic using StratoQL, a domain-specific, structurally typed language inspired by Scala's core (records, variants, pattern matching) and Facebook's Haxl. Key features include:
  - Direct native support for Apache Thrift data types without code generation.
  - Language restrictions to prevent infinite loops, unbounded memory usage, and heavyweight compute.
  - Built-in transparent concurrency and automatic request batching for asynchronous downstream RPC queries.
  - Runtime first-class types enabling automatic serialization and high-level interfaces, such as a centralized GraphQL layer for mobile clients.

### Takeaways
- Extreme decentralization generates hidden costs: duplicated infrastructure setup, orphaned services, and barriers to applying cross-cutting policies.
- Architectural "sweet spots" exist where generic capabilities with standardized interfaces (like compute scheduling or RPC transports) can be centralized without restricting product velocity.
- Domain-specific languages and purpose-built microservice platforms like Strato demonstrate that thoughtfully constraining developer runtimes can provide massive systemic leverage while preserving autonomous feature delivery.

talks.title: "Categories for the Working Hacker" by Philip Wadler
talks.teaser: Shows how products, sums and exponentials from category theory map onto records, variant types and functions in code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the Curry-Howard correspondence, which links logical proofs with types in programming. The speaker argues that category theory forms a third member of this correspondence, so the same structures describe logic, lambda calculus and categories. He introduces the basic vocabulary of objects, arrows, identities and composition, and illustrates it with monoids, which are structures with an identity and an associative operation.

The middle section covers the core data structures. A product corresponds to conjunction and to records or pairs, and the number of values in a product is the product of the sizes of its parts. The speaker shows the idea in Java and then in a shorter Haskell version. A sum corresponds to disjunction and to tagged unions, such as an error message or a number, consumed with a case expression. An exponential is a function type, and counting its values gives the exponent. Flipping the arrows swaps products and sums, a duality that gives the same ideas in reverse.

The closing section connects these structures to blockchain languages, including Simplicity and Michelson, and to Plutus, which is built on System F omega. The talk ends by deriving an exponential law that matches an identity from high school algebra. The speaker encourages listeners to learn category theory first and to treat painful Java-style code as a sign that a cleaner abstraction exists.

talks.title: "A Tale of Two Asyncs: Open Source Language Design in Rust and Node.js" by Ashley Williams
talks.teaser: Traces how the async designs of Node.js and Rust were shaped by their goals, values and open-source governance.
talks.summary:
Ashley Williams compares how Node.js and Rust approached asynchronous programming, arguing that a language's design is shaped by the goals and values behind it rather than by inevitable technical trends. She frames the talk with ideas from the history of philosophy, treating programming languages as historical artifacts. Node.js grew out of the C10K problem, where servers struggled with many simultaneous connections. Its creator made an event loop and callbacks the core model, with non-blocking I/O as the main design goal.

Rust was built first around memory safety and later extended toward server-side work. Its asynchronous stack layers the mio low-level I/O library beneath futures, with Tokio combining them into a reactor. The speaker describes a practical surprise: async Rust code compiled and passed the lints but did nothing, because the event loop had to be started explicitly. She also explains how Rust uses domain working groups, public RFCs and gradual syntax changes, such as the move toward the question-mark operator for error handling, to balance ergonomics against productivity.

The talk closes by arguing that projects need a clearly articulated shared vision. It cites the Vasa warship and C++ governance debates as examples of feature creep without coherence. She suggests that JavaScript has drifted from its original goal of being an easy-to-use scripting language, and urges language communities to state their visions and gather broader feedback.

talks.title: "Your Secrets are Safe with Julia: A Compiler for Secure Computation" by Jason Dagit
talks.teaser: Explains how a Julia-to-circuit compiler uses symbolic execution and homomorphic encryption to run programs on encrypted data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Strange Loop, Jason Dagit discusses an IARPA-funded proof-of-concept project conducted at Galois to address the usability challenges of secure computation, specifically homomorphic encryption (HE). While homomorphic encryption enables computation directly on encrypted data without decrypting it, it faces two primary hurdles: massive performance overhead (5 to 10 orders of magnitude slower than native CPU execution) and significant programming difficulty, as computations must ultimately be expressed as arithmetic circuits (integer polynomials). Dagit and his team focused on the usability problem by building a compilation toolchain allowing programmers to write standard Julia code and automatically compiling it into arithmetic circuits evaluated via an HE backend.

### Key Topics
- **Homomorphic Encryption Basics**: The structure of HE evaluated over integer rings supporting associative, commutative addition and commutative multiplication, but lacking general division, dynamic control flow, and persistent memory.
- **Symbolic Execution with Crucible**: Using Galois' open-source symbolic evaluation framework, Crucible (written in Haskell), to interpret and unroll high-level Julia programs into arithmetic circuits and polynomial expressions.
- **Integration with Palisade**: Utilizing Palisade, a lattice cryptography library developed by Kurt Roloff and his team at the New Jersey Institute of Technology, to execute arithmetic circuits over encrypted data.
- **Data Flattening and Metadata**: Managing dynamic structures such as matrices by enforcing concrete dimensions while allowing symbolic elements, flattening structures into integer arrays, and generating Julia metadata functions to reshape decrypted output.

### Technical Details
The toolchain workflow begins with standard Julia code (such as an image-sharpening algorithm or linear regression). By using Julia’s reflection capabilities, the system lowers the abstract syntax tree (AST) into an S-expression representation without needing a custom parser. This AST is handed to Crucible, which symbolically evaluates the program with designated symbolic inputs and concrete dimensions (e.g., fully unrolling loops and eliminating side effects like dead error paths).
Crucible outputs an arithmetic circuit along with Julia metadata functions designed to rebuild structured data types from flat integer lists. The data is encrypted using Palisade, evaluated homomorphically through Palisade's circuit interpreter, and the resulting ciphertext is returned to Julia for decryption and reshaping. Dagit also noted specific technical limitations and discoveries: division was restricted to power-of-two right shifts as the final operation on a ciphertext; large circuits required streaming out of Crucible to prevent Haskell heap exhaustion; and loops with symbolic bounds (like Euclid's GCD) cannot be easily bounded. Furthermore, the functional specifications derived via symbolic execution enabled equivalence verification between algorithms (such as naive determinant vs. Richard Bird's integer-only determinant) using SMT/SAT solvers.

### Takeaways
The project demonstrated that symbolic execution is an effective bridge between high-level dynamic programming languages and the rigid, polynomial representations required by homomorphic encryption backends. While this proof of concept specifically targeted usability rather than the underlying cryptographic performance penalties, it highlighted how formal methods, symbolic evaluation, and solver-based equivalence checking can make privacy-preserving computation accessible to domain scientists.

talks.title: "Data Driven UIs, Incrementally" by Yaron Minsky
talks.teaser: Shows how incremental computation keeps data-heavy web interfaces fast by updating only the parts that changed.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a dense, data-heavy trading interface: a table of around a hundred thousand rows that stays responsive while values update, sorting and filtering are applied. The speaker, whose trading firm builds its internal tools in OCaml, argues that such interfaces are really incremental computation problems, where only what changed should be recomputed. He presents the familiar model, render and action loop used by Elm and React, and locates the costly work in the render step.

The middle of the talk covers an incremental library his firm built, which records a dependency graph of a computation and refires only the affected parts when inputs change. He walks through the map, map2 and bind combinators, with bind enabling dynamic graphs. Those prove insufficient for large collections, so he builds a diff-based map using a symmetric diff over persistent maps, then a nested variant that splits and joins a map so each entry gets its own pipeline.

He closes by urging developers to treat UI design as an algorithms problem, separating a clean functional description of the interface from the efficient machinery behind it, and to consider self-adjusting computation as a practical tool. Diff and patch recur throughout, from the virtual DOM to network protocols. The example application is available as open source.

talks.title: "Making Games for 1920s Hardware" by Mike Lazer-Walker
talks.teaser: Shows how a 1927 telephone switchboard keypad became a playable time-management game using modern electronics and software.
talks.summary:
Mike Lazer-Walker presents Hello Operator, a time management game built around a 1927 Western Electric 551A switchboard keypad. He walks through bringing an old, locked device back into working order: a colleague measured the lock and 3D printed a key, and the wiring was traced with continuity testers because the switches activated in unusual ways. Replacing the original incandescent lamps with LEDs created a new problem, since the old wiring could not be chained like modern addressable LEDs. The roughly 70 lamps and switches also needed more input and output ports than a single microcontroller offered.

The middle of the talk covers the software. Cheap microcontroller clones were combined with a Mac Mini, and cable connections were detected by setting every port as an input and pulling one at a time low, a technique similar to keyboard key matrices. The game logic was kept separate from the hardware behind a single output interface, so the same engine could run on an iPad, from a command line, or on the physical panel. Streaming the game's internal state over WebSocket to an iPad app helped diagnose a faulty device in about half an hour. A separate board game with an Alexa companion used a similar state-machine design, which made it testable without publishing.

The closing section argues that physical form shapes how people experience a system, and that games built on real-world skills draw players in. The speaker encourages developers to reuse the tools they already know to build unconventional interfaces without first learning a new engineering discipline.

talks.title: "Why I chose to modularize the ducks in my React App" by Lauren Lee
talks.teaser: Walks through restructuring a Redux codebase by bundling actions, constants and reducers into a single Ducks module.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a former English teacher who moved into software engineering, describes joining a team that maintained a web app for curating a weekly top-twenty list. The app was built with Mustache and Handlebars, and its code had grown into one long, tangled HTML file that the team called a kludge. Instead of refactoring, the manager approved a full rewrite. The team chose React for its component model and virtual DOM, then covered its drawbacks, mainly that state passed through several layers of props becomes hard to keep in sync.

Redux was introduced as the answer, with a single store, pure reducers, and actions and action creators that describe state changes. A demo app listing popular TV shows showed the common organization by type, where constants, actions and reducers live in separate folders, so a small feature means jumping between files. The speaker then moved to the Ducks pattern, which bundles the action types, action creators and reducer for one feature into a single module. She refactored the demo live and noted that reducers should return new state with methods such as concat rather than mutating arrays with push.

The closing section argued that Ducks makes it clear which code handles which feature and cuts down on scrolling through files. Because the Redux logic stays separate from the React view layer, the state library could be swapped more easily. The speaker stressed that Ducks is only one structure among many and encouraged teams to choose the layout that suits their code.

talks.title: "Democratizing AI - Back-fitting end-to-end machine learning" by Joel Young and Bo Long
talks.teaser: Describes how LinkedIn is rebuilding its machine learning stack to speed up model development, deployment and monitoring.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Joel Young (lead of the Machine Inference Infrastructure team) and Bo Long (lead of the Machine Learning Algorithms team) present LinkedIn's journey to completely rethink and modernize their machine learning infrastructure through the "Productive ML" initiative. As AI powers core LinkedIn products—such as People You May Know, feed ranking, job recommendations, LinkedIn Learning, Sales Navigator, Recruiter, and internal systems like anti-abuse and build failure routing—prior custom-built stacks led to substantial technical debt and "second system syndrome." With machine learning democratizing across engineering disciplines, LinkedIn needed an extensible architecture to eliminate friction, prevent ivory-tower silos, and more than double modeler productivity by accelerating experimentation iteration speed while keeping serving costs low.

### Key Topics
- **Democratization of ML**: Supporting engineers across product and UI teams who have practical ML skills, moving away from reliance on dedicated ML specialists.
- **Extensible Architecture**: Avoiding lock-in to single frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) by structuring the system across modular layers: experimentation/authoring, training clusters, packaging, and production serving.
- **Feature Marketplace**: A centralized hub enabling discoverability, metadata tracking, feature selection, and online/offline feature consistency.
- **Modeling as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)**: Representing ML models as DAGs consisting of feature transformations, deep embeddings, and trainable scoring components.
- **Model Training Ecosystem**: Utilizing deep learning (TensorFlow), boosted trees (XGBoost), and generalized linear mixed models via the open-sourced Photon ML library.
- **Health Assurance & Monitoring**: Continuous offline/online validation, automated drift tracking, anomaly detection on deployments, and threshold-triggered retraining.
- **People and Organization**: Implementing a "team of teams" organizational model, establishing the AI Academy (including training for managers), and deliberately managing incremental adoption to avoid the "support trap."

### Technical Details
- **Quasar DSL**: Rather than using graphical drag-and-drop tools, LinkedIn developed Quasar (Quick Ass Scoring and Ranking), an in-house declarative domain-specific language that handles complex vector operations, cosine similarity, tree-based scoring, and first-order list operations (top-k, filtering, diversity).
- **Photon ML & Mixed Models**: LinkedIn employs generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) via Photon ML to scale personalized recommendations. To manage large-scale user/item interactions across 500 million members and 10 million jobs, training combines a global model (e.g., XGBoost trees over deep neural embeddings) with localized per-user and per-job linear models.
- **Serving Architecture**: Instead of computing brute-force pairwise interactions (500M members × 10M jobs), serving breaks down by context: per-member coefficients are retrieved by a mid-tier service from an online key-value store, while per-job coefficients live in sharded forward indices on search nodes. The Quasar inference engine executes scoring directly on searchers using columnar modes and vector batching for real-time responsiveness.
- **Frame Platform**: Enforces parity between offline training data and online inference signals through unified libraries and shared configurations, preventing data discrepancies.
- **Auto-tuning**: Uses Gaussian process-based methods to automate hyperparameter tuning over vast feature and parameter spaces.

### Takeaways
- Speeding up model iteration coupled with early feedback directly drives improvements in product metrics.
- Modeling abstractions should separate semantic feature definitions from storage/runtime anchors to support multi-environment deployment.
- Early lifecycle validation significantly reduces production maintenance overhead; proactive anomaly detection and automated retraining outperform arbitrary fixed schedules (e.g., weekly cron jobs).
- To deploy large platform updates successfully, organizations should roll out components incrementally (pre-alpha to GA) to protect engineering teams from the "support trap" of overwhelming maintenance costs.

talks.title: "Making machines that make music" by Srihari Sriraman
talks.teaser: Shows how software can model and generate South Indian classical music, from raga grammar to Markov chains over ornamented notes.
talks.summary:
Srihari Sriraman, a software consultant and vocalist, describes several years of work on getting software to produce South Indian classical music. He starts with the basics: a tonic reference pitch, swaras as pitch numbers relative to that tonic, and ragas as melodic grammars with separate ascending and descending scales. Standard notation alone misses the continuous slides and ornaments that define the style, so he models each ornament as a frequency curve and renders phrases that sound much closer to the real music.

To learn the grammar from data, he gathers recordings from online sources, extracts pitch with an autocorrelation tool, cleans up noisy live recordings, and finds the tonic by picking the strongest peak in a pitch histogram. First-order Markov chains over note transitions improve the output, but higher-order chains only produce long strings of ornaments with no clear tonal shape. Studying tala cycles shows that tonal patterns sit at the half-beat level and ornaments at finer subdivisions, so generating at those levels and adding simple repetition gives more melodic results, though organic repetition remains hard to model.

The work also yields by-products: raga identification by comparing a sung phrase against known pitch profiles, and automatic notation of sung input. The talk closes with an open question about whether machine-generated music can count as art when listeners tend to connect music with the artist. The main takeaway is that time and context are central to modelling melody, and that machines switch between musical grammars far more easily than humans do.

talks.title: "Design and Implementation of a Topic Detection System" by Wes Chow
talks.teaser: Shows how a word co-occurrence graph and community detection can surface local events from short tweets in production.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents a topic detection system built to surface local events from Twitter, run as a production tool rather than a theoretical design. Geotagged tweets are collected for a region and processed in hourly batches over the trailing 24 hours. Only the tweet text is kept, with retweets noted. The talk first reviews why common approaches such as k-means, LDA and NMF struggle with very short messages, since a single tweet offers too little word overlap to compare.

The chosen method builds a graph in which words are nodes and edges are weighted by the tweets where two words co-occur. Very frequent words are filtered out, along with edges that appear in only one tweet, and the Louvain community detection algorithm, which optimizes modularity, finds clusters of words that form events without a preset number of topics. On a day of Boston tweets, examples include traffic, a political race involving Elizabeth Warren, and a congressional primary win. Dropping retweets surfaces more hyperlocal stories, such as a hurricane's approach. Each cluster gets a representative tweet chosen by cosine similarity, which the speaker says works reasonably about 60% of the time. A day of data for one city processes in two to three seconds on one core.

The closing section covers limitations: clusters are mutually exclusive, modularity tends to overlook small clusters, and talk radio yields larger, less meaningful clusters. Planned work includes overlapping communities, conductance-based measures, and better evaluation for tuning the resolution parameter. The talk ends with a case for network models over vector-space methods for language analysis.

talks.title: "Misuser" by David Schmudde
talks.teaser: Shows how artists who misuse networks, web pages and animation tools expose value and flaws that engineers overlook.
talks.summary:
David Schmudde opens by contrasting a painted pipe with a real one to show that a tool has a purpose it can fail, while an artwork resists being pinned down. He argues that artists have long pushed tools beyond their designers' intent, from drum machines in hip-hop to new painting methods, and that this creative misuse often reveals how a system really behaves. He also draws on C. P. Snow's warning about the gap between science and the arts.

Next he walks through historical examples. An early business network from the 1970s and 1980s opened accounts to artists, who wrote a community story on it that had little commercial value but showed the network's edges. Web art from 1995 exploited page source views, a slow-rendering blink-tag page, and a browser bug that allowed animation before Flash existed. At Bell Labs, Lillian Schwartz's animation work pushed a language beyond its design, leading to new features that were later used for research and education. An artist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory had a glitch-driven grid that engineers then fixed by adding randomness. A 2018 piece built entirely in CSS was tested across older rendering engines to check robustness. A Brazilian videotext piece from the 1980s now runs only as an emulation, which changed its meaning.

He concludes that technology includes code, design, social relationships, education and culture, not just the screen or the network. His takeaway for engineers is to bring artists in early and treat misuse and edge cases as useful information about robustness and human experience.

talks.title: "Running With Scissors: Live Coding With Data" by Stuart Halloway
talks.teaser: Shows a REPL-driven Clojure workflow that uses live data, generated examples and spec to explore and test code interactively.
talks.summary:
Stuart Halloway opens by looking at Clojure's rise and then asks what a developer should do once they sit down at the keyboard with a program in mind. He breaks the REPL into its read, eval and print functions and argues that a shell which does not evaluate code the same way a real program does leaves developers working in a different environment.

He presents a task-specific style he calls running with scissors: start from example data, load only the namespaces a function needs, and use spec to generate sample inputs instead of one hand-written case. He recommends inspecting data in spreadsheets or charts rather than raw printouts, keeping rich comment blocks at the bottom of files as a durable record of the development process, and writing tests as replayed REPL sessions with checks. He contrasts modeling data as generic maps with namespaced keys, which merge easily across sources, against rigid per-entity structs, and compares targeted form-level redefinition with project-wide reloading and graphical debuggers that offer little programmability.

In the final section he applies spec to an existing Clojure wrapper around a Java charting library, writing predicates for axis sizes and ordering, generating random charts, and enabling instrumentation only during development. Within a minute of generative testing he found a bug in the JVM itself. The takeaway is to live inside the running program and invoke tools from there, using generated data alongside examples.

talks.title: "Chasing the Stream Processing Utopia" by Kartik Paramasivam
talks.teaser: Describes what an ideal stream processing platform needs, covering exactly-once, scaling, local state, SQL and tooling.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Kartik Paramasivam, manager of near real-time data processing and streams infrastructure at LinkedIn, outlines the vision for an ideal "utopia" in stream processing. At LinkedIn, streaming infrastructure processes more than a petabyte of data and trillions of messages daily using Apache Kafka for pub/sub messaging and Apache Samza for stream processing. Stream processing is employed across varied domains including social computing, bot detection, application monitoring, and security monitoring. Paramasivam identifies the fundamental requirements for reaching an ideal stream processing world: empowering developers to build applications of any complexity, operate at any scale, ingest data from any source, code in their language of choice, deploy in any environment, and leverage robust tooling.

### Key Topics
- **Application Complexity and Patterns**: Examining the shift from simple stateless operations (filtering, transformation) to complex stream-table joins and stateful aggregations (windowing, tumbling windows). Addressing accuracy challenges such as exactly-once processing (EOP) across ingestion, processing, and storage sink tiers.
- **Scaling Ingestion and Clusters**: Operating large-scale distributed message queues using Apache Kafka, managing bare-metal cluster sizing (limiting clusters to 125–150 nodes), multi-cluster federation, disk failure resilience without broker crashes, and automated cluster rebalancing with Kafka Cruise Control.
- **Scaling Stream Processing and State Management**: Mitigating I/O bottlenecks in data access through asynchronous calls, batching, caching, and local materialized caches (via change data capture systems like Brooklin). Implementing high-performance local state storage using RocksDB, incremental checkpointing, and host affinity in Apache Hadoop YARN.
- **Unifying Batch and Stream Sources**: Using HDFS as a stream input source with an "end of stream" concept to seamlessly execute streaming applications as batch jobs for model evaluation and historical experimentation.
- **Accessibility through Polyglot APIs and SQL**: Lowering the barrier to entry via Apache Calcite SQL, converting legacy Hive and Pig scripts to stream processing topologies, and integrating Apache Beam for Python support.
- **Ecosystem Tooling and Observability**: Bridging the tooling gap between batch and stream processing with pipeline visibility, schema management, lag monitoring, and health tracking using tools like Burrow and Kafka Monitor.

### Technical Details
- **State and Data Enrichment**: When joining streaming data with databases like LinkedIn's homegrown Espresso, relying on remote RPC lookups risks denial-of-service on upstream databases. Samza introduces a remote `Table` abstraction incorporating async I/O, caching, and rate limiting, as well as a local table approach backed by Brooklin change capture streams and partitioned local RocksDB instances. Local state yields roughly 100x to 200x faster lookups compared to remote databases.
- **Reliability and Host Affinity**: Samza coordinates with YARN to guarantee container host affinity, ensuring that stateful tasks reattach to their existing RocksDB data upon restart or upgrade, while replaying state changes from Kafka changelog topics only when needed. Full-snapshot checkpoints fail at gigabyte and terabyte scale, making incremental checkpoints mandatory.
- **Exactly-Once Semantics**: Handled across three stages: (1) ingestion deduplication using deterministic client IDs, (2) pipeline processing deduplication using techniques like Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshotting rather than heavier transaction models, and (3) storage persistence using idempotent writes or transactional database capabilities.
- **Ingestion Operational Engineering**: LinkedIn avoided RAID redundancy overhead on Kafka by updating Kafka brokers to tolerate individual disk failures. Cluster operational overhead is automated via Kafka Cruise Control, which balances traffic across brokers without saturating network interface cards (NICs).

### Takeaways
Achieving stream processing utopia requires moving beyond basic stream-processing primitives toward higher-level abstractions. Critical enablers include declarative SQL (via Apache Calcite), unified batch and streaming models (via Apache Beam and HDFS end-of-stream triggers), managed stream processing as a service with automated resource tuning, and self-healing cluster and pipeline operational tools such as Kafka Cruise Control, Burrow, and Kafka Monitor.

talks.title: "The Hard Parts of Open Source" by Evan Czaplicki
talks.teaser: Examines why open-source communities turn hostile, tracing the ideas behind them and proposing ways to design healthier discussions.
talks.summary:
Elm's designer Evan Czaplicki opens with seven years of maintaining an open-source language and argues that keeping a friendly community is one of the hardest parts of such projects. He lists recurring patterns: suggestions that ignore hidden trade-offs, the expectation that someone will absorb unpaid criticism, and challenges to who has the authority to decide. A long Clojure forum thread, in which that language's creator described the emotional cost of harsh replies on his weekends, illustrates the toll on maintainers.

To explain these dynamics, he traces an intellectual history running from Norbert Wiener's cybernetics and the Whole Earth Catalog to early Electronic Frontier Foundation thinking and a hacker manifesto written after an arrest. He then connects that history to Edward Bernays's public relations campaigns and the idea of nudges, citing Google's colour-coded cafeteria food and muted ad labels as examples of choice architecture. Engagement-driven design, he argues, rewards viral outrage and pushes people into shared spaces where they lose context, such as clashing programming communities or accounts with no visible identity.

His alternative is intentional communication. A poster declares a purpose such as learning or self-expression, and the reply tools then guide the exchange through flows like asking for clarification, answering, or thanking. Feedback becomes more specific, with labels describing whether a post is helpful or confusing, rather than a blunt downvote. He closes by urging developers to build communities whose design matches their goals, and to consider whether their tools serve people or simply drive engagement.

talks.title: "Generating Music From Emotion (and other experiments)" by Hannah Davis
talks.teaser: Shows how emotion data can drive music and image generation, and why labeled datasets matter.
talks.summary:
Hannah Davis opens with data sonification, which turns data into sound, and separates direct conversion, parameter mapping and music generation. She explains why sound suits streams, cycles and emotional impact.

Her main project, Transprose, uses a word-emotion lexicon to trace emotion across a novel and raise melodic movement at emotional peaks, so the music follows the emotional arc rather than literal events. She plays examples from several novels and then shares other experiments: emotion curves from the 2016 presidential debates, a piece built from news articles and orchestrated with a French composer, a UFO sightings dataset whose evening clustering set a rhythm, and an early soundtrack generator for video. A sound installation in a former Italian factory used clustering of recorded sounds to guide its pieces.

Auditing the lexicon revealed words such as childbirth tagged with no emotion, which led her to study subjective data. She crowd-labelled a set of Flickr landscapes with emotions, finding for example that fear often attached to forests and open ocean, then used style transfer to move scenes between emotions. As a scholar at OpenAI she also generated emotional variations of landscapes. The closing argument is that datasets encode cultural values, so they should carry labels about their origin and limits.

talks.title: "To Serve The People: Public Interest Technologists" by Matt Mitchell
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "To Serve The People: Public Interest Technologists" by Matt Mitchell.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, technologist and hacker Matt Mitchell discusses the emergence and necessity of "Public Interest Technologists." Drawing parallels to the evolution of public interest law funded by philanthropic institutions in the 1960s and 1970s, Mitchell addresses the brain drain of engineering talent toward large commercial tech companies. He challenges developers and security practitioners to examine whether their daily work aligns with their values and details practical avenues—including grants, fellowships, specialized conferences, and corporate volunteer policies—for technologists to support civil society, marginalized communities, human rights defenders, and investigative journalists.

### Key Topics
- **Aligning Work with Personal Values**: Mitchell shares his personal journey from early hacking and roles at CNN and The New York Times to realizing his technical skills could directly protect vulnerable populations. Key catalyst events included the killing of Trayvon Martin, the Edward Snowden surveillance revelations, and the killing of Michael Brown.
- **Grassroots Digital Security and Crypto Harlem**: Mitchell recounts creating Crypto Harlem in a neighborhood community center to teach practical encryption and digital safety to local residents, analogizing encryption to essential literacy.
- **The Public Interest Technologist Model**: Exploring how funding consortia like NetGain (comprising the Ford Foundation, MacArthur Foundation, Knight Foundation, Open Society Foundations, and Mozilla) invest millions to embed technologists in civil society, public policy, and government.
- **Funding and Grant Opportunities**: Practical options for technologists wanting to launch open-source, public-interest tools, highlighting the Open Technology Fund (OTF), Open Knowledge International, and Fight for the Future's A-Teams.
- **Fellowships and Policy Integration**: Fellowships providing pathways into social impact work, such as the Mozilla Open Web Fellowship, TechCongress, Code for America, Institute for the Future, and New America's Cybersecurity Initiative.
- **Alternative Engagement Paths**: Engaging through global conferences (such as RightsCon, Chaos Computer Club, Internet Freedom Festival, and Allied Media Conference) or utilizing corporate paid volunteer time and pro bono allowances at existing employers.

### Technical Details
- **Signal and Cryptographic Funding**: Mitchell highlights Signal's initial support from the Open Technology Fund, noting how its double ratchet encryption scheme became a foundational privacy technology subsequently adopted and paid for by platforms like WhatsApp and Google to maintain Signal as a free tool.
- **Operational and Tactical Security Training**: Mitchell's work with Global Journalist Security involves operational security (OpSec) and InfoSec drills simulating high-stress scenarios (hostile environments, phishing, phone spoofing, and physical kidnapping) to prepare reporters and activists.
- **Zero-Day Discovery in Civil Society**: Mitchell details a case study from Access Now's digital safety helpdesk. Mexican activists working on a soda tax campaign received suspicious messages, which Access Now escalated to Citizen Lab in Toronto. Citizen Lab identified an undisclosed iOS exploit sold by NSO Group (costing around $650,000 for ten targets) that gave attackers remote access to the camera and microphone. The finding was responsibly disclosed to Apple, which patched the zero-day vulnerability.
- **Secure Tooling Ecosystem**: The talk emphasizes supporting tools critical to activist safety, including Tails OS, Tor, encrypted communication systems, and hardening application security against targeted surveillance.

### Takeaways
- Technologists possess outsized leverage through software and security expertise, which can be applied to defend civil liberties and at-risk communities.
- A robust ecosystem of grants (OTF, Open Knowledge) and fellowships (Mozilla, TechCongress, Ford Foundation) exists to financially support technical contributors outside Big Tech.
- Direct involvement does not require quitting a job immediately; engineers can contribute via conferences, open-source bug fixes, UX design improvements for privacy tools, and employer-sponsored volunteer programs.

talks.title: "Zuul's Journey to Non-Blocking" by Arthur Gonigberg
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix moved its Zuul edge gateway to non-blocking Netty and RxJava, and when that move pays off.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Arthur Gonigberg presents Netflix's architectural migration of its edge proxy service, Zuul, from a blocking Java servlet model to a non-blocking, asynchronous architecture. Zuul operates as the front door to Netflix on AWS, managing tens of billions of requests per day and handling critical functions including routing, security (DDoS mitigation and blocking fraudulent traffic), monitoring, and resiliency. While initial micro-benchmarks showed dramatic throughput increases (up to 73,000 requests per second), real-world production performance between Zuul 1 and Zuul 2 showed only a modest 10% to 20% throughput gain. The talk explores how Netflix executed the rewrite, the severe engineering and operational pitfalls encountered, and the distinct resiliency and architectural benefits achieved.

### Key Topics
- **Zuul 1 Architecture & Limitations**: Zuul 1 ran on Tomcat with standard Java servlets using one thread per request. Latency spikes at origins or connection spikes caused rapid thread pool exhaustion and severe cascading failures during traffic surges.
- **Building Blocks of Non-Blocking Systems**: The shift required non-blocking I/O primitives (e.g., epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD), an asynchronous programming paradigm (RxJava), and an event loop framework (Netty).
- **Incremental Migration via Zuul 1.5**: To safely replace the engine while serving massive production traffic, Netflix first adopted Tomcat's APR connector to decouple connections from requests, then converted the filter chain to return observables (`applyAsync`), allowing filter execution in both Tomcat and Netty.
- **Zuul 2 Architecture**: Netty server fronting incoming requests, Netty client managing outbound proxying, and an RxJava filter chain stitched in between on single-threaded event loops.

### Technical Details & Operational Pitfalls
- **Blocking Shared Libraries**: Shared platform libraries often made blocking calls (such as `Thread.sleep`), which paused Netty event loop threads and stalled hundreds of concurrent requests. Netflix used `reactive-audit` to detect blocking calls at runtime.
- **ThreadLocal State Corruption & The 'Geo Shuffle'**: Netty event loop threads multiplex many requests. Shared libraries relying on `ThreadLocal` storage leaked state between requests. A severe production bug dubbed the 'Geo Shuffle' occurred when geo-lookup IP data was stored in thread locals, causing San Francisco users to be assigned geo-data for Siberia, Brazil, or South Africa and routed to remote CDNs. The fix required explicitly copying and setting channel state onto thread locals upon entering Netty channel pipelines or RxJava threads.
- **Direct Memory Leaks**: Netty utilizes off-heap direct memory via JNI and epoll. Incomplete request lifecycles caused gradual direct memory leaks that silently brought server traffic to zero RPS without throwing traditional heap errors.
- **Debugging & The Request Passport**: Standard thread dumps and stack traces were ineffective in async code. Netflix truncated repetitive RxJava stack traces, disabled trace generation in high-CPU critical paths, and implemented the 'Request Passport' (inspired by Zach Hellman) to record timestamped channel state transitions to debug complex timing issues and ELB timeouts.

### Takeaways & Guidance
- **Workload Profiles Matter**: Zuul is fundamentally CPU-bound due to authentication, encryption, decryption, and hashing. Non-blocking models do not reduce core CPU processing requirements; hence, CPU-bound workloads see minimal throughput improvements (10–20%). In contrast, I/O-bound services, large file streams, chat systems, or push notification architectures benefit heavily.
- **Resiliency Benefits**: Zuul 2 excelled during 'retry storms' (when failing clients rapidly retry, outstripping auto-scaling capacity). Instead of aggressively throttling legitimate traffic, Zuul 2 handled significantly higher RPS at max CPU and safely dropped retries when origin error thresholds were breached.
- **Expanded Capabilities**: Zuul 2 comfortably handles tens of thousands of concurrent connections per instance, enabling WebSocket support for push notifications and removing the need for strict timeouts and Hystrix circuit breakers.

talks.teaser: Traces a personal chatbot project from early text-based game experiments through its Ruby design, language processing and live demo.

Coraline Ada Ehmke traces the history of Alice, a chatbot she has built and extended since the mid-1990s. The story starts with text-based social environments, where her first bot, Budge, answered questions about a virtual museum of Egyptian artifacts, and Ghouls, which listened to conversations and replayed phrases that drew responses. Alice later moved into a private IRC channel and then a Slack community of about seventy members.

The middle of the talk walks through the architecture. Alice is a Ruby application with a single Sinatra route, MongoDB storage and a newer Neo4j graph database. Each message passes through a listener, a processor, a commander and a mediator. Commands are matched either by a simple parser or by a natural language step backed by Google's NLP API. Context objects let Alice follow the topic or user under discussion, and she gathers facts from Wikipedia and web search, ranking them by a declarative index. The live demo covered a text dungeon with generated rooms, items, a map, brewed beverages and a grue that devours players, along with questions answered from context.

The closing section looks at planned work: parsing stored facts to answer questions, generating sentences from parts of speech with Markov chains, and a separate project, Sophia, that models concepts such as temperature using ranked expressions with synonyms and antonyms. The takeaway is that a playful side project can teach practical NLP ideas, and that play supports learning.

talks.title: "Kotlin: Uncovered" by Victoria Gonda
talks.teaser: Shows how Kotlin features such as data classes and null safety look once compiled Kotlin bytecode is decompiled back to Java.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces Kotlin as a statically typed language for the JVM that interoperates with Java. Because Kotlin compiles to bytecode, that output can be decompiled back into Java to reveal what the compiler generates. Starting with a simple user class, the decompiled code shows a final class, private fields, null checks on constructor parameters and generated accessors.

Data classes add componentN functions, copy, toString, equals and hashCode, along with synthetic methods for default parameter values. For null safety, calling a method on an unchecked nullable value does not compile, the safe-call operator becomes a null-guarded ternary, and the double-bang operator becomes an explicit check that throws a null pointer exception. The Elvis operator becomes a conditional return. Delegation is illustrated with a copy-printer example from a blog post, where the generated class forwards calls to delegate objects. Extension functions compile to static methods in a utility class, and lambdas passed to inline functions are placed at the call site, while a non-inline lambda becomes its own class.

The talk ends by showing how to open the Kotlin bytecode view and decompile code in IntelliJ or Android Studio, and how to convert Java files to Kotlin while reviewing double-bang operators. The speaker argues that reading the generated code clarifies what language features cost, and that working in Kotlin has made them more attentive to nulls.

talks.teaser: Demonstrates how TLA+ model checking exposes race conditions in a banking transfer design before any code is written.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that concurrency bugs resist the usual tools. Unit tests multiply combinatorially when timing-dependent systems interact, and type systems or pure functions cannot stop outside services from crashing mid-operation. A simple bank transfer with an overdraft rule shows the problem: two concurrent transfers can overdraft an account, and a crash between steps can duplicate money.

The speaker models the transfer in TLA+, a formal specification language, and checks an invariant that no account goes negative. The model checker, TLC, explores every interleaving of the steps. Adding a second concurrent transfer produces a counterexample trace showing how one transfer's balance check passes before the other's subtraction lands. Running the steps inside a single database transaction fixes the violation, and the fix is confirmed before any code is written. Three workplace cases follow: an app installer where the model caught an overlapping-worker bug, a zero-downtime deployment spec used as compact design documentation for another team, and a message-processing change that broke earlier invariants and exposed a gap in the team's understanding, leading them to relax older requirements.

The takeaway is that a specification validates a design rather than the code, so implementations still need careful checking, but design flaws can surface early. The talk closes with resources for learning TLA+ and PlusCal, from an introductory tutorial to Lamport's canonical book and a text on the temporal logic underneath.
