talks.title: "Controlling Time and Space: understanding the many formulations of FRP" by Evan Czaplicki
talks.teaser: Maps the many formulations of functional reactive programming, from Elm's static signal graphs to arrowized and higher-order designs.
talks.summary:
Elm's designer untangles the many meanings of functional reactive programming. He starts with first-order FRP as used in Elm, where signals are wired straight to the outside world, such as mouse position and key presses, and are transformed, accumulated over time and merged into a graph. Static, always-running, synchronous graphs make architecture, hot swapping and time-travel debugging practical.

Later variants relax these constraints. Higher-order FRP lets the graph be reconfigured through a join operation, but switching to a signal that needs its full past can cause unbounded memory growth, so research restricts the types to rule that out. Asynchronous data flow, found in Reactive Extensions and Bacon.js, lets signals end and be flattened, trading away default synchrony and raising questions about hot and cold signals. Arrowized FRP, seen in Yampa, netwire and Elm's automaton library, uses automata detached from world inputs, which suits structuring code.

No variant wins outright, since each trades features against others. The closing advice is to judge them by the properties an application needs: synchrony by default, asynchrony for network or disk work, reconfigurable graphs, direct world inputs, debugging tools, and code that stays clear as it grows.

talks.title: "Building Real-time Systems with Open Source Technologies" by Gian Merlino and Fangjin Yang
talks.teaser: Walks through a real-time analytics stack built from Kafka, Storm, Hadoop and Druid for querying fresh event data.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both engineers at the ad-tech startup Metamarkets, describe building a real-time analytics stack for interactively exploring large volumes of time series event data. They explain why relational databases, precomputing key-value stores, and plain Hadoop MapReduce queries fell short for business intelligence style aggregation at scale. They then describe adopting Druid, an open source column store that rolls up data, splits it into immutable time-based segments, and answers queries quickly across many nodes.

The middle of the talk layers in streaming components. Events arrive through an HTTP API into Kafka, Storm cleans, transforms and joins them using windowed reductions, and real-time indexers feed Druid so queries reflect events within seconds. The speakers are candid about the trade-offs: late corrections are hard to apply, and short join windows leave a small share of records unmatched. To address this they add a Hadoop batch path that reprocesses older data, a lambda-style design, with the Druid broker merging results from all three layers.

The closing section lists the open source projects and connectors that glue the pieces together, and sums up the roles: Kafka for transport, Storm and Hadoop for preparation, Druid for serving. The takeaway for practitioners is that a fresh, queryable analytics pipeline can be assembled from existing open source parts. A Q&A covers Druid's pluggable deep storage, with S3 or HDFS as the usual choices, and its lack of precomputation, which it replaces with fast scanning and filtering.

talks.title: "Production Prolog" by Michael Hendricks
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from running Prolog in production, covering its debugger, useful libraries, and the trade-offs the team found.
talks.summary:
This talk is an experience report on using Prolog, a logic programming language, in production for about eighteen months at a shop that runs many languages. The speaker starts with the basics: the execution model rests on unification, backtracking and lazy search, code is stored as data in a database, and one predicate can often run in several directions, so a short relationship definition can answer many different questions.

The middle of the talk covers the tooling and libraries the team relies on. SWI-Prolog was chosen largely for its open-source development tools, especially a debugger that lets you edit code mid-run and retry a failed call from an earlier point. The speaker also points to Mercury's bisecting debugger as an idea that could be brought to Prolog. Other examples include a static checker that team libraries can extend, packs for function-style syntax and optional runtime type checks, constraint-based date and calendar logic, and concurrency wired up automatically from data flow. Saved states, which bundle a compiled program into one file for deployment, and a reversible bencode parser round out the examples.

The closing section lists the downsides: a small ecosystem with fewer tools such as static analysis, a learning curve for developers used to imperative code, failure messages that give little explanation, hard-to-debug macros, and performance costs that only occasionally surface. The takeaway is that the language rewards declarative thinking, but a team has to be willing to invest time before it pays off.

talks.title: "Nashorn: implementing a dynamic language runtime on JVM in 2014" by Attila Szegedi
talks.teaser: Explains how Nashorn speeds up JavaScript on the JVM using optimistic typing and on-the-fly recompilation.
talks.summary:
Nashorn is the JavaScript runtime that ships with Java 8. It runs on the JVM and is developed in the open in the OpenJDK repository. The talk explains why a fast dynamic language runtime is hard to build and reports on the performance work done for later Java releases, with benchmark comparisons against the older Rhino engine and against V8. The speaker concedes that V8 is still faster in many cases, but says number-crunching performance had caught up considerably.

The middle of the talk covers the main optimizations. Nashorn compiles separate versions of a function for different parameter types. It uses optimistic typing, assuming values are integers and recompiling when that assumption fails, and it widens integer arithmetic to long when overflow occurs. To deoptimize running code without relying on VM-specific tricks, it throws an exception, catches it at the call site through an invokedynamic try-catch combinator, and resumes execution in a generated continuation method. Static type inference within a function, careful handling of local variables across try and catch blocks, and dead-code elimination reduce how often recompilation is needed.

The closing section looks at future plans. The team wants to extract these techniques into a reusable library, a kind of LLVM for dynamic languages on the JVM, with an intermediate code representation that sits between JavaScript and bytecode. The main takeaway is that the JVM's strict bytecode verification shapes how dynamic language engines must be designed.

talks.title: "Art.js: Transfigure Data to Create 21st Century Art" by Sarah Groff Palermo
talks.teaser: Explores data art as a creative practice distinct from data visualization, with examples built in JavaScript and D3.
talks.summary:
Sarah Groff Palermo, a designer who taught herself to code, argues that data art differs from data visualization. Traditional visualization seeks comprehensive datasets to communicate what has been found, while data art works with small, fragmented, personal data to express an experience. She gives four reasons to make it: understanding oneself, understanding the systems people live within, broadening one's data skills, and because it is fun.

The examples fall into two groups. The literary approach treats data like a novel. First Chapters draws novel openings as connected sentence lengths, a taxi project replays one New York cab driver's shift, Quantified Breakup charts an artist's divorce through bubble and line charts, and the speaker's own timeline of neglect shows unread books decaying over time. The language-based group includes Patatap, a keyboard-driven sound animation, a patent generator that writes applications for classic literature, and Matthew Connelly's analysis of redaction patterns in government documents to suggest FOIA requests.

For process, she recommends sketching, gathering rough data even by hand, testing repeatedly, and sharing the work. Ideas can start from a personal interest, from a tool such as D3 layouts or the topo time library, or from translating an artwork into data. In the question period she suggested guiding viewers from a simple overview to an interactive sandbox, so artistic framing and statistical depth can coexist.

talks.title: "Idris: Practical Dependent Types with Practical Examples" by Brian McKenna
talks.teaser: Shows how dependent types in Idris can prove algebraic laws, check inputs and bound computational cost at compile time.
talks.summary:
Brian McKenna opens with the seL4 kernel, a formally verified kernel running on a drone. He contrasts its workflow, with proofs in Isabelle, a high-level Haskell layer and hand-written C, with older attempts at extraction from Coq, where Peano numbers, unsafe coercions and a shell script patching generated output made the process fragile. Idris is presented as a dependently typed language that compiles to executables, and he shows idium, a window manager written in Idris with a small Objective-C layer for the macOS API.

The middle of the talk is live coding. He starts with a bitwise OR on a single bit type and proves it is associative, letting proof search fill in simple goals and using the tactic language to rewrite with the earlier result. He then extends the proof to bit strings. Next, he defines a binary character type indexed by its value, so a string only typechecks as binary digits when evidence for every character is supplied, and a bad literal fails to compile. The final example tracks computation cost in the type. A cost-indexed monad adds costs on bind, a recursive day-by-day computation is shown to have factorial cost, and a bounded Fin type prevents running it beyond six.

He closes by arguing that proofs can raise confidence in algorithms, types can encode input rules and resource limits, and examples can be checked by the compiler instead of by separate tests. He notes that the cost bind is asserted rather than verified, that Idris has known bugs, and that it should not yet be used in production.

talks.title: "Testing Distributed Systems w/ Deterministic Simulation" by Will Wilson
talks.teaser: Shows how deterministic simulation lets engineers reproduce and hunt rare distributed system bugs that random failures hide.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from why distributed systems are so hard to debug. Timing, packet loss and disk behavior are outside the programmer's control, so a failure may vanish on the next run and a fix cannot be verified. The speaker presents deterministic simulation as the answer: an entire cluster runs inside a single process, with networks and disks replaced by simulated versions whose randomness comes from a seeded generator, so every run can be repeated exactly.

He describes the pieces this requires. Code is written in Flow, a C++ extension that lets developers write actor-style concurrency while running single-threaded. Simulated networks inject latency, dropped connections and read errors. Test files pair a workload, such as a ring-of-keys invariant that exposes atomicity or isolation failures, with faults like clogged connections, rolling reboots, configuration changes, simulated failing disks and swapped hardware. Techniques such as bugification, time acceleration and correlated failures modeled on heavy-tailed statistics help surface rare bugs faster than customers would. Some runs are executed twice to catch hidden nondeterminism, and millions of simulations run each night.

The talk ends with the limits. Debugging often falls back to print statements, the simulation is only as accurate as the team's understanding of operating systems and hardware, and third-party code such as ZooKeeper cannot be simulated. A physical test cluster of programmable power supplies complements the simulator and exposed bugs in outside software. The main takeaway is that determinism makes bugs reproducible and fixes verifiable, but it should be paired with real-world testing.

talks.title: "Type Systems - The Good, Bad and Ugly" by Paul Snively and Amanda Laucher
talks.teaser: Walks through what separates good type systems from bad ones, from Curry-Howard and dependent types to syntax and culture.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shared goal of writing better software and argues that type systems vary widely in quality. The speakers frame a good type system as one that makes the desired path the effortless one, and that lets developers make illegal states unrepresentable. They note that even developers in dynamically typed languages reason about types in their heads, so the real question is how much of that reasoning a checker can take over.

The middle of the talk covers the features that separate strong systems from weak ones. Sum types with pattern matching, product types, parametric polymorphism, extensibility and type inference are discussed, along with the Curry-Howard correspondence, which treats a type as a theorem and a function as its proof. A dependent-type example on vector append shows code that fails to compile when sizes do not line up. Weak systems are illustrated with stringly typed code, false positives from structural typing, and type systems that mainly block correct programs and force casting. Syntax, tooling and community are presented as equally important to the type system itself.

The talk closes with an informal hierarchy of type systems, moving from basic correctness through expressivity to dependent types, and points to the Lambda Cube as a way to compare them. The takeaway for practitioners is to ask what is at stake when a program misbehaves and to pick type-system strength to match. The speakers also say that dependent-type languages are not yet production-ready, so the field still has considerable room to develop.

talks.title: "The Sociology of Programming Languages" by Leo Meyerovich
talks.teaser: Examines how programming languages spread and get adopted, using survey and repository data and diffusion-of-innovation theory.
talks.summary:
The talk treats programming languages as social systems rather than purely technical artifacts. The speaker argues that designers often optimize for speed, safety and expressiveness, while adoption depends on how easily people can try a language, see others using it and fit it into existing work. Drawing on an ecological model of adoption, languages spread through overlapping groups of users and grow niche by niche.

To test these ideas, the speaker's group analyzed a survey of about 13,000 people rating languages, a follow-up survey of roughly 15,600 developers about their real projects, a smaller online-course sample, and about a quarter million SourceForge projects. Languages clustered into niches: Java spread broadly, while Scheme appeared in narrower areas such as build tools. Usage formed a long tail, suggesting room for smaller languages to sustain communities. Respondents mostly chose languages for libraries and familiarity with their team or existing code rather than speed or safety. Most people knew about four languages well, mainstream languages took months to learn, and C and C++ took years.

The talk then draws on diffusion of innovation research, including a 1980s safe-sex campaign that enlisted visible opinion leaders and gave them observable markers. Trialability, observability, relative advantage and compatibility emerge as useful lenses for language design, with examples such as Stack Overflow's network effects. The speaker closes by suggesting that teams use collective usage data, such as traces from real programs, to guide tooling like code hinting and test generation.

talks.title: "React: RESTful UI Rendering" by Pete Hunt
talks.teaser: Applies REST architecture constraints to browser UI design, comparing distributed systems history with how React renders interfaces.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of distributed systems, moving from message passing and MPI to distributed object systems such as CORBA and RMI. The speaker argues that these object systems hid network behavior behind local-looking calls, which made systems slow, fragile and hard to predict. The talk then introduces REST as a set of constraints, including client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, layering and a uniform interface, meant to yield performance, simplicity, visibility and reliability.

The middle of the talk compares this history to front-end development. Early browser code mixed rendering, data storage and event handling, and MVC-style fine-grained change observation produced cascading, order-dependent updates. To address this, Facebook built React, where components return a description of the desired interface, that description is diffed against the previous one, and only the necessary DOM operations are applied. The speaker maps React's event system, explicit state transitions and optional caching through shouldComponentUpdate onto the same REST principles, with an example of a component that caches its render output.

The closing section argues that these principles are general software design guidance rather than something specific to one library, and gives examples such as Unix pipes and DNS. The speaker also contends that web components keep duplicated state in the DOM and so fall short of these properties. The practical takeaway is to apply the constraints to one's own problem domain, keeping state explicit and interactions predictable.

talks.title: "Transducers" by Rich Hickey
talks.teaser: Shows how transducers decouple map and filter logic from collections, channels and streams so the same steps can be reused.
talks.summary:
Rich Hickey introduces transducers, a way to pull the core logic out of map, filter and similar sequence functions so it can be reused. He argues that these functions keep being rewritten for collections, streams, observables and channels, each time with different rules. His proposed fix is to describe each step as a process transformation that wraps a reducing function, leaving out the details of the data source and destination.

To make this concrete, he uses a luggage-handling example: unbundling pallets, removing food bags, and labelling heavy bags, composed into one reusable instruction set. The same composed transducer then runs in several contexts, including pouring into a collection, producing lazy sequences, summing bag weights with a reduce, and flowing through channels. He explains why composition looks backwards, since the steps are built right to left but execute left to right. He also covers early termination through a reduced wrapper, completion for flushing stateful steps, and an optional init arity.

The closing takeaway is that a transducer is more primitive than the collection version, so a team can define a transformation once and get support in any context that accepts transducers. Hickey notes that stateful transducers must create fresh state each time they are applied, and he leaves the type-system design as an open problem for language implementers.

talks.title: "Inside the Wolfram Language" by Stephen Wolfram
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a symbolic programming language with built-in knowledge, instant cloud APIs, and lessons from decades of language design.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Wolfram Language, a symbolic programming language the speaker has developed over roughly 35 years, building on Mathematica and Wolfram Alpha. Its design packs curated knowledge and automation directly into the language, which by now has about 5,000 built-in functions. Much of the session is a live demonstration on a desktop instance, covering image processing, sound synthesis, network graphs, geographic queries and entity lookups such as planetary data.

The demos show natural-language entry for real-world entities, a small image classifier trained on paintings from two artists, and the idea that code, documents and interfaces are all symbolic expressions transformed by pattern rules. The speaker then shows how a function can be deployed as a web form, a REST API, or embedded code for other languages, and touches on parallel kernels and a data drop mechanism for device data.

Toward the end the speaker reflects on language design, including careful function naming, the tension between precise design and heuristic natural-language design, and using design work to force a deep understanding of a domain. The takeaway is that the language aims to shorten the path from an idea to a deployed product and offers an approachable way to learn programming through short, working examples.

talks.title: "Programming Should Eat Itself" by Nada Amin
talks.teaser: Shows how a reflective Scheme interpreter tower lets each meta level redefine the one below it, with live demos.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether a language's evaluator can be made reflective, so that each level in a tower of interpreters defines the level above it and can be changed independently. It builds on the idea from SICP that the evaluator is itself just a program. To explore this, the speaker uses a reflective Scheme system called Black, whose code comes from a 1996 paper.

Live in the demo, the speaker moves up and down the meta levels by triggering errors and by exiting explicitly, and inspects user-level definitions from a lower level with a base evaluator. She then redefines the application step so that a chosen symbol behaves as a special form, and shows that the meta level can host instrumentation that counts function applications. This is used to compare two Church-numeral predecessor encodings, where one is far more efficient. Last, she demonstrates the "there and back again" pattern for zip and reverse, rebuilding the call stack as a data structure.

The speaker frames the work as programming to understand programming rather than to ship software, and notes that the approach is not meant for practical use. She sketches a later OCaml implementation based on a paper on meta-continuations, where types make lifting continuations easier to get right. Ideas for future work include adding types to the object language, F-expressions, and generative compilation in Scala. The takeaway is a method: start from a paper, implement it concretely, then extend it.
